entry.title: CDS joins you don't read: does HANA really skip them? (measured)
entry.content:
In my last post I checked if a WHERE on top of a CDS table function really reaches the table. This one goes the other way. Your view has three joins, and the consumer reads only one or two fields. Does HANA still execute all the joins?

Most of us answer this from memory: "HANA prunes unused joins", or "only with associations", or "only if you declare the cardinality". I wanted to see the plans, so I built a small lab on two releases.

The question

A view joins MARA with MAKT (texts) and T134 (material types). A report selects only the material number. Which joins does HANA really execute? And what happens to the result when the cardinality you declared is not true?

The setup

  • Systems: S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758, HANA 2.00.073) and S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755, HANA 2.00.052), both lab systems.
  • Data: the standard tables with the demo data that was already there. 2023: 1,199 materials and 2,051 material texts in 3 languages. 2020: 2,566 materials and 19,885 material texts in many languages.
  • Eight CDS view entities on MARA, changing only how the join is written:
  • ZJP_OUTER: LEFT OUTER JOIN to MAKT (language 'E' in the ON condition) and to T134, no cardinality.
  • ZJP_TOONE: the same with LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_ASSOC: the same with association [0..1] and a path in the field list.
  • ZJP_INNER: INNER JOIN to T134.
  • ZJP_VIEW_OUTER: LEFT OUTER JOIN to a view entity on T134 instead of the table (VDM style), no cardinality.
  • ZJP_VIEW_TOONE: the same with LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_TEXT: LEFT OUTER JOIN to MAKT without the language, no cardinality. One row per material and language, and the view says so.
  • ZJP_TEXT_ONE: association [0..1] to MAKT without the language. This cardinality is a lie: a material has one text per language.
  • Three consumer statements per view, in ABAP SQL: only Material, Material plus one joined field, and COUNT(*).
  • Method: rows counted in ABAP. For the plans I looked up the statement that ABAP SQL really sent in the HANA SQL plan cache and ran EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SQL PLAN CACHE ENTRY via ADBC. So each plan belongs to the real ABAP statement, not to a native SQL I typed by hand.

The results

Both releases gave the same plans. Rows are shown as 2023 / 2020.

ViewOnly MaterialMaterial + joined fieldCOUNT(*)Tables in the plan, only Material
ZJP_OUTER, no cardinality1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_TOONE, to one1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_ASSOC, [0..1]1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_VIEW_OUTER, join to a view1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_VIEW_TOONE1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_INNER1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA, T134
ZJP_TEXT, no language, no cardinality2,051 / 19,8852,051 / 19,8852,051 / 19,885MARA, MAKT
ZJP_TEXT_ONE, no language, [0..1]1,199 / 2,5662,051 / 19,8851,199 / 2,566MARA

The COUNT(*) plans follow the same pattern: MARA alone, except ZJP_INNER and ZJP_TEXT. With Material plus the text, ZJP_OUTER joins MAKT and still leaves T134 out.

Look at the last line. Same view, same WHERE (none), and the number of rows depends on the fields the consumer selects.

What the plans show

Simplified excerpts from the 2023 system. The 2020 system shows COLUMN SEARCH on MARA instead of TABLE SCAN, with the same tables.

ZJP_OUTER, only Material. Both joins are gone:

SELECT /* FDA READ */ "MATERIAL" FROM "ZJP_OUTER" WHERE "MANDT" = ?

PROJECT
  TABLE SCAN MARA

ZJP_OUTER, Material and text. MAKT comes back, T134 stays out:

COLUMN SEARCH
  JOIN
    COLUMN TABLE MARA
    COLUMN TABLE MAKT

ZJP_INNER, only Material. The join stays, because an inner join can remove rows:

COLUMN SEARCH
  JOIN
    COLUMN TABLE MARA
    COLUMN TABLE T134

ZJP_TEXT_ONE: with only Material, HANA reads MARA alone and returns 2,566 rows on 2020. Add the text and the join comes back with 19,885 rows, about 7.7 times more.

Where the cardinality goes

The SQL that activation generates for each view (ADT shows it) was the same on both releases:

  • LEFT OUTER JOIN without cardinality stays LEFT OUTER JOIN.
  • LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN and association [0..1] both become LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_TEXT_ONE also becomes LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN, with only MANDT and MATNR in the ON condition. HANA has no way to know that this is false, so it trusts it.

Does anyone warn you?

  • 2023, association [0..1] without the language: activation passes with warning DD_CDS_ANALYSIS 302, "Cardinality 1 of Association _TEXT does not match to the ON-condition".
  • 2023, the same mistake written as LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN: no cardinality warning in the syntax check.
  • 2020: no warning for either version. The message text exists in the 2020 system, but the check did not fire for this view.

So the only warning I got was on the newer release, only for the association, and it is a warning: the view activates and runs.

Takeaways

  • HANA drops a LEFT OUTER JOIN you don't read when it can prove the join returns at most one row. Here it got that proof in two ways: the ON condition covered the whole primary key of the joined table (ZJP_OUTER needed no cardinality at all), or I declared it (TO ONE or [0..1]). A simple view entity in between did not stop it. My reading is that HANA used the primary keys of MAKT and T134; I did not test a join that is unique in the data but not by key.
  • An INNER JOIN is never dropped, even when you read nothing from it, because it can remove rows. If the lookup is optional, LEFT OUTER is not only the right semantics, it also lets HANA skip it.
  • When HANA cannot prove "to one" (ZJP_TEXT), it keeps the join. That is the safe default.
  • When you declare "to one" and it is not true, HANA believes you. The row count then depends on which fields the consumer selects: a list with the text shows 19,885 lines, the COUNT(*) on the same view says 2,566. For text associations, put the language in the ON condition (usually $session.system_language).

About time: with these small tables, the difference between a dropped and a kept join was below 1 ms per query and inside the noise of 10 runs, so I am not using time as the argument here. The gain grows with the size of the dropped tables, which I did not measure. The lie was visible in time on 2020: 3.7 ms for the 2,566 rows against 66.7 ms for the 19,885 rows (average of 10 runs with GET RUN TIME, including the transfer to ABAP).

The code

Views, with the annotations removed:

define view entity ZJP_OUTER
  as select from mara
    left outer join makt on  makt.matnr = mara.matnr
                         and makt.spras = 'E'
    left outer join t134 on t134.mtart = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      makt.maktx as MaterialText,
      t134.mtref as ReferenceType
}

// ZJP_TOONE: the same, with "left outer to one join" in both joins.

define view entity ZJP_ASSOC
  as select from mara
  association [0..1] to makt as _Text on  _Text.matnr = $projection.Material
                                      and _Text.spras = 'E'
  association [0..1] to t134 as _Type on _Type.mtart = $projection.MaterialType
{
  key mara.matnr  as Material,
      mara.mtart  as MaterialType,
      _Text.maktx as MaterialText,
      _Type.mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_INNER
  as select from mara
    inner join t134 on t134.mtart = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      t134.mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_TYPE
  as select from t134
{
  key mtart as MaterialType,
      mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_VIEW_OUTER
  as select from mara
    left outer join ZJP_TYPE as Typ on Typ.MaterialType = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr        as Material,
      mara.mtart        as MaterialType,
      Typ.ReferenceType as ReferenceType
}

// ZJP_VIEW_TOONE: the same, with "left outer to one join".

define view entity ZJP_TEXT
  as select from mara
    left outer join makt on makt.matnr = mara.matnr
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
  key makt.spras as Language,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      makt.maktx as MaterialText
}

define view entity ZJP_TEXT_ONE        // the lie: no language in the ON condition
  as select from mara
  association [0..1] to makt as _Text on _Text.matnr = $projection.Material
{
  key mara.matnr  as Material,
      mara.mtart  as MaterialType,
      _Text.maktx as MaterialText
}

How I read the plan of the real ABAP statement:

SELECT material FROM zjp_outer INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_rows).   " the consumer

" ADBC: find the statement in the plan cache and explain the cached plan
DATA(lo_st) = cl_sql_connection=>get_connection( )->create_statement( ).
" SELECT PLAN_ID FROM M_SQL_PLAN_CACHE
"  WHERE STATEMENT_STRING LIKE '%"ZJP_OUTER"%'
lo_st->execute_update( |EXPLAIN PLAN SET STATEMENT_NAME = 'JP1'| &&
                       | FOR SQL PLAN CACHE ENTRY { lv_plan_id }| ).
" SELECT OPERATOR_NAME, TABLE_NAME FROM EXPLAIN_PLAN_TABLE
"  WHERE STATEMENT_NAME = 'JP1'

Caveats

  • Two releases, lab systems, small demo data, one client each. I could not reach a 2025 system (SAP_BASIS 816) for this round.
  • Simple joins only. The view on the right side was a plain projection. VDM views with unions, aggregations or their own joins on the right side were not tested.
  • The LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN version of the lie was only syntax checked, not activated and run. That syntax generates the same MANY TO ONE join (see ZJP_TOONE), so I expect the same behavior, but I did not measure it.
  • Plans come from EXPLAIN PLAN (the optimizer). I did not use PlanViz.
  • HANA Cloud and the BTP ABAP Environment were not tested.

Your turn

Have you seen a "to one" join that HANA did not drop? Or a KPI that did not match the list behind it because of a cardinality? I would like to compare notes, especially on 2025 and on HANA Cloud.

entry.title: Local AI models for ABAP: what you gain and what you pay (measured)
entry.content:
Two reasons keep coming up for running an AI model locally for ABAP work: the client's code never leaves your machine, and there is no bill per token. Both are good reasons. Before recommending it to anyone, I wanted a few numbers from a normal developer PC, not from a 128 GB workstation.

The setup

  • My PC: Ryzen 7 5700X, 24 GB RAM, Radeon RX 580 with 8 GB (an old card; Ollama runs it through Vulkan).
  • Ollama 0.35, local models at temperature 0.
  • Two systems to judge the code: S/4HANA 2023 (ABAP 7.58) and S/4HANA 2020 (ABAP 7.55).

1. Speed: what "zero cost" looks like on this PC

ModelFile sizeTokens per second
ABAP fine-tune, 3B (8-bit)3.3 GB17.3
qwen2.5-coder 7B (4-bit)4.7 GB12.5
qwen2.5-coder 14B (4-bit)9.0 GB5.5

A correct answer to the tasks below is 200 to 900 tokens. With the 7B that is 15 to 70 seconds per answer, with the 14B 40 seconds to almost 3 minutes. The 14B does not fit in 8 GB of video memory: Ollama put a third of it on the CPU (66% GPU, 34% CPU), and that is where the speed goes. I did not try a 32B model: it needs around 20 GB, and this PC has 24 GB of RAM in total.

So there is no bill per token, but the cost does not disappear. It moves to hardware and to waiting time.

2. Quality: does the ABAP compile, and is it right?

I wrote 9 small tasks that look like daily work:

  1. A SALV report on SFLIGHT (the same request as in a local AI tutorial here in the Community)
  2. Last day of the month (date logic)
  3. Sum an internal table by key, modern syntax
  4. ABAP SQL count with a range
  5. Materials with texts, keeping materials without a text (LEFT OUTER JOIN)
  6. ALPHA conversion (leading zeros)
  7. An AMDP method in SQLScript
  8. A CDS view entity with an association and a filtered path
  9. ABAP Cloud: read products through the released API, not table MARA

The judge is the SAP system, not me:

  • Each answer is checked by the ABAP compiler. If there are errors, the compiler message goes back to the model, up to 3 times.
  • The code that compiles is activated, and hidden ABAP Unit tests (the model never sees them) check the result.
  • Task 9 also runs ATC with the variant ABAP_CLOUD_READINESS.
  • Before measuring any model, I tested the judge itself: a correct solution passes every task, and known bugs fail. For example, the language filter in the WHERE instead of the ON turns the outer join into an inner join, and the test catches it.

The local model here is a small ABAP fine-tune (Qwen2 architecture, 3.1B parameters, 8-bit). It fits completely in the graphics card, which is the realistic size for a normal PC. As a reference line I ran the same tasks with a cloud model (Claude Sonnet 5.5).

ModelSystemCompiles at first tryCompiles after compiler feedbackCorrect (hidden tests)
ABAP fine-tune, 3B (local)20232 of 92 of 90 of 9
Claude Sonnet 5.5 (cloud)20238 of 99 of 99 of 9
Claude Sonnet 5.5 (cloud)20207 of 88 of 88 of 8

(Task 9 is only in the 2023 run: ABAP Cloud on-premise starts with S/4HANA 2022.)

How the small model failed is worth a look:

  • Report: it read a table FLIGHTS (the table is SFLIGHT) and called a function module ALV_GRID_DISPLAY that does not exist, with invented parameters. Then it repeated i_grid_border_radius_... until it hit the token limit.
  • Date: it compiled at first try, with a fixed list of month lengths. February always has 28 days, and the month is read from the wrong position of the date. All 5 tests failed.
  • AMDP: it declared the marker interface and then wrote ev_count = SELECT COUNT(*) FROM MARA WHERE MANDT = iv_mandt. That is neither SQLScript nor ABAP.
  • Compiler feedback: it did not help. In the 7 tasks that never compiled, the model answered the compiler message at least twice by sending back exactly the same code.

The cloud model also made one mistake: in the report it forgot the @ before a host variable. The compiler caught it, and the model fixed it in one round.

3. Local is not automatically private

I checked four things on my PC:

  • Where Ollama listens. By default only on 127.0.0.1:11434, and that is what I found. If you set OLLAMA_HOST to 0.0.0.0, anyone on your network can use it.
  • Which websites can call it. The default list is localhost and the editor webviews. One tutorial here sets OLLAMA_ORIGINS="*". With that, any website open in your browser can send prompts to your local model and read the answers.
  • Cloud models. Ollama now also serves cloud models. My server config shows OLLAMA_REMOTES = ollama.com and OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD = false. If you pick a cloud model by mistake, the prompt leaves your machine. OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 switches that off.
  • What leaves during generation. I listed the TCP connections of the Ollama processes while the model was writing: nothing outside the machine. Your editor extension is a separate program, with its own settings and telemetry. Check it too.

And one that has nothing to do with AI: if your SAP password sits in plain text in the editor settings file, that is the leak.

My take

  • If the client's code cannot leave your machine, local is the right direction. The privacy argument is real.
  • A small model that fits a normal graphics card does not write correct ABAP by itself. In this test: 0 of 9.
  • The compiler loop catches mistakes, but it cannot add knowledge. It fixed the cloud model's one slip in one round, and it did not move the small model at all.
  • Whatever model you use, the compiler and a test have to see the code before you trust it.
  • If you go local, use the biggest model your hardware runs at a speed you accept, and check the four points above before you connect it to anything.

Caveats

  • One run per task: local models at temperature 0, the cloud model with its default settings. Another run could give other answers.
  • The small model was measured only on 2023, and its answers were cut at 1,500 tokens (the longest correct answer was under 900).
  • For the 7B and the 14B I measured only speed, on a short answer of about 120 tokens. Their ABAP quality is not in this post.
  • The tasks are small, one object each. No RAP, no enhancements.
  • I could not test Joule, so it is not in the comparison.
  • The cloud model is the reference line, not a recommendation.

Your turn

Are you using a local model for ABAP? Which model, on what hardware, and for what kind of work?

entry.title: From clean core level to decision: reading what a custom program actually does (part 3)
entry.content:
Disclosure: I'm the author of this post and the creator of Clean-Core.io, a free, non-commercial community tool. This post is educational and describes a method you can apply by hand; the tool is optional and complementary to SAP ADT/ATC and the SAP toolchain, not a replacement.

In part 1 we graded each dependency of a custom object on SAP's clean core levels A–D. In part 2 we turned that into visibility and two KPIs. Both answer how far a piece of code is from a clean core.

Neither answers the question that decides the effort: what does this program do for the business, and should it be kept, rebuilt or retired? This part is about reading that from the code.

The business rules are in the IF statements

A grown Z-program is often the only up-to-date description of a process. Two passages from a fictitious purchase requisition approval report:

"Plant 1000 is the central warehouse
IF gs_eban-werks = '1000'.        " line 87
  gv_skip_limit = abap_true.
ENDIF.

"Tolerance agreed with purchasing
IF lv_dev_pct > 5.               " line 412
  PERFORM hold_for_buyer.
  RETURN.
ENDIF.

Neither is a clean core violation. Both are business rules: plant 1000 skips the approval limit, and a price more than 5 % above the reference goes to a buyer. Whatever happens to the program, these two rules have to survive, or someone has to decide on purpose that they don't. No ATC check tells you that. The code does.

A reading flow

Step Look for Write down

1. Entry pointsSTART-OF-SELECTION, selection-screen events, dialog modules, public methods, function modulesthe line
2. Dataevery SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, MODIFY, DELETE on own or SAP tablesthe line, read or write
3. Business rulesIF / CASE on business values: plant, document type, amount, tolerancethe line, the condition in plain words
4. EffectsRFC, update tasks, BAPIs, mails, files, messagesthe line
5. Gapsdynamic calls with a variable target, includes you don't have"not determined", with the reason

Draw the result as a process. BPMN works well because a key user can read it. Anchor every task and gateway to its line: a step that can't point back to a line is an opinion, and a gap you write down is an open question rather than a wrong answer.

Then add what parts 1 and 2 gave you: each SAP object with its level and how it is used. Reading EBAN is a different matter from updating it; a direct write to an SAP table stays a problem whatever the table's own level. And run ATC in your system: it is the check that counts.

From the reading to a decision

Option When it fits

RetireNobody needs the process any more. Usage data helps here.
Move to SAP standardThe standard covers the process; each custom rule maps to configuration or is dropped on purpose.
RebuildThe rules are still needed. Rebuild in-app on ABAP Cloud where the logic belongs to the core, side-by-side on SAP BTP where it is loosely coupled or mainly talks to other systems.
Keep for nowWith the risk and a review date written down.

One thing that is easy to get wrong: a classic construct is not by itself a reason to move a program off the stack. A batch input, a piece of native SQL or a local RFC call is something to replace with a released API inside a rebuilt in-app solution. Side-by-side pays off when the logic itself is independent of the core, not because one statement is old.

Record which option you chose, on which evidence (the lines, the levels, ATC), under which assumptions, and who confirmed it. Six months later, that record is what makes the decision reviewable.

What the reading gives the next step

  • Target design: which SAP objects the new code reads through released APIs or CDS views. Part 1 used KNA1 → I_Customer; for EBAN, look up the released purchase requisition API for your release on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.
  • A first code draft that carries both rules over, for a developer to review in ADT and check with ATC and the Clean ABAP style guide.
  • Test cases from the same rules, so "plant 1000 skips the limit" is a test, not tribal knowledge.
  • The process as a BPMN 2.0 file for whoever documents the to-be process, for example in SAP Signavio.

Where this stops

  • The code shows the process the code implements. Customizing, jobs and manual steps around it are not in it.
  • Static reading can't resolve every dynamic call. Say so instead of guessing.
  • The levels come from SAP's published data; ATC in your target system has the final word.
  • Generated code, from any tool or model, is a draft for a developer to review.

Conclusion

Levels and scores tell you how far a program is from a clean core. The decision about the program needs one more thing: what it does, line by line, with its business rules made visible. Read that first, and "we have a lot of Z-code" turns into a list of decisions you can defend.

How do you get from a clean core level to a decision per program today: key-user workshops, a decision log, something else? And where has reading the code misled you?

entry.title: Building on the ADT REST API: 8 silent traps I measured (and how to defend against each)
entry.content:
Over the last months I have been building tooling, and AI agents, that work with ABAP systems through the ADT REST API, the same HTTP API that Eclipse uses. And I noticed a pattern: most of my bugs were not in my code. They were places where the API answers 200, or "finished", or an empty list, and something else happened.

More and more people are building on this API now (agents, CI pipelines, custom tools), so I'm sharing the eight traps that cost me the most, each one measured again for this post in an S/4HANA 2023 system (SAP_BASIS 7.58). For each one: what you see, why it happens, the proof, and the defense.

1. "Finished" is not "clean"

What you see: you start an ATC run, the API answers HTTP 200 and the run is finished. Looks like a green light.

Why: the run status tells you the run ended, nothing about the code. The result lives in the worklist, and you have to go and read it.

Proof: I ran ATC on a test table whose log setting is wrong on purpose. The run finished normally. Then the worklist (GET /sap/bc/adt/atc/worklists/{id}) had this inside the object:

<atcfinding:finding ... atcfinding:priority="1" atcfinding:messageId="0022" .../>

(message 0022: change log active although the data class is APPL0 or APPL1), and an empty <atcworklist:infos/>.

Defense: after every run, fetch the worklist and count findings by priority. And read infos too: that's where checks that could not run show up. A check that didn't run is "not checked", never "clean".

2. A syntax check that didn't happen

What you see: you send source to the check run API and get zero messages back.

Why: if the object doesn't exist yet, the check isn't processed at all. Zero messages, because nothing was checked.

Proof: a check run with an artifact for a class that doesn't exist came back with chkrun:status="notProcessed" and the text "Ressource CLASS ... existiert nicht", and no messages.

Defense: read chkrun:status before reading the messages. Zero messages with notProcessed means "unknown", and a tool that reports it as "no syntax errors" is lying with a straight face.

3. Checking loose source uses default program attributes

What you see: a perfectly normal SELECT fails the syntax check of a draft program, and then works in the real one.

Why: "fixed point arithmetic" is a program attribute. When you check source for a program that doesn't exist yet, the check runs without it, while a program created in SE38 or ADT gets it switched on by default, and classes always have it.

Proof: the same SELECT, with a JOIN and an inline @DATA( ):

  • checked as a new program: "This ABAP SQL statement uses additions that can only be used when the fixed point arithmetic flag is activated", plus a follow-up error for the inline table;
  • checked inside an existing class: zero errors.

Defense: check code in the context of a real object (an existing class, or a shell in $TMP). When an error depends on a program attribute, treat it as a context problem, not as broken code.

4. Data preview: 255 characters per line, and 36 runs per session

This one is two traps with the same root, and the root is in the ADT code itself.

What you see: a long SQL in the data preview (/sap/bc/adt/datapreview/freestyle) is refused with "Maximum number of character exceeds 255 in line 1". And in a long stateful session, after many previews, you suddenly get an HTTP 500 saying that the maximum number of temporary subroutine pools was exceeded.

Why: the data preview compiles your query. Class CL_ADT_DP_OPEN_SQL_HANDLER, method generate_subroutine, splits the query at line breaks, refuses any line longer than 255 characters, writes a small program around it (class main, method EXECUTE_CODE) and runs GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL. The ABAP documentation of that statement explains the rest: a source line can't exceed 255 characters, an internal session can create at most 36 temporary subroutine pools, and they are never released until the session ends.

Proof: the 255 check is in the method above, with its own text element; the GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL is a few lines below; and I got the HTTP 500 after a series of previews in the same stateful session.

Defense:

  • send SQL with line breaks, never one long line;
  • don't run data previews in a stateful session that lives forever: use stateless requests, or start a new session before you get near 36.

5. An empty where-used list proves nothing

What you see: the where-used of a class comes back empty, or almost empty, and you conclude nobody uses it.

Why: the where-used list reads an index. For your own objects it's updated when you activate them, but the index for SAP objects is built by a separate job, which isn't always run after an installation.

Proof: in my system /UI2/CL_JSON calls cl_abap_typedescr=>describe_by_... in 16 lines. The global where-used index (WBCROSSGT) has zero entries for that pair. It has 611,981 rows in total, and only 69 for CL_ABAP_TYPEDESCR, a class the standard uses everywhere.

Defense: before you say "unused", run a positive control: take one usage that you know exists and check that the index finds it. If it doesn't, fall back to a source search.

6. Parse the element, not the value

What you see: your tool reads that every table type in the system is "sorted" (or "standard", or "unique"), no matter what.

Why: many ADT object bodies carry the editor's dropdowns. A table type body has the real value in <ttyp:accessType>standard</ttyp:accessType>, and next to it a <ttyp:valueHelps> block with every possible value: standard, sorted, hashed, unique, nonUnique...

Proof: in the body I read for this post, that block is more than half of the 5 KB. Bonus: its labels came in German, while my session was in Portuguese.

Defense: use a real XML parser and read the element that carries the value. A regex looking for the value anywhere in the body will match the dropdown and return a plausible, wrong answer for every object. And don't rely on the language of the labels.

7. A filter that is silently ignored

What you see: you call a list (named item) collection with filter=... and get a short list back, so the filter worked. Or did it?

Why: in these collections maxItemCount is applied on the server, but filter can be ignored without any error.

Proof: /sap/bc/adt/repository/informationsystem/objecttypes?maxItemCount=3, and the same call with &filter=ZZZNAOEXISTEMESMO (Portuguese for "really doesn't exist"), returned identical bodies, the same three items byte for byte. I had seen the same before on 7.56 and 8.16 systems.

Defense: test every filter parameter with a value that can't match anything. If you still get items, filter on the client side.

8. 406 means "wrong Accept", not "not there"

What you see: HTTP 406 on an endpoint, and you conclude the feature doesn't exist in that system.

Why: ADT negotiates the content type strictly. A 406 says the endpoint exists and doesn't serve the media type you asked for.

Proof: /sap/bc/adt/feeds with Accept: application/xml → 406, and the message lists the accepted type: application/atom+xml;type=feed. With that header: 200.

Defense: read the media types from /sap/bc/adt/discovery and from the 406 message itself before concluding anything is missing.

One more, if you are building agents

Everything that comes back from the system is data: source code, long texts, message texts, table contents. Any user can type a sentence into a document text. An agent that reads it must treat it as content to analyse, never as an instruction to follow.

The common thread

All eight have the same shape: the API answers successfully, and the meaning of the answer is somewhere else. My rule now is simple: for every "OK" a tool reports, it must be able to say what it read that proves it. "Finished", "200", "zero messages" and "empty list" are not proof of anything on their own.

If you have hit others, I'd love to hear them in the comments.

entry.title: Custom columns in VA05 on S/4HANA: what the code does with your BAdI
entry.content:
"How do I add my own fields to VA05?" keeps coming back in the forum. In S/4HANA, VA05 runs report SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_VIEW, which is a small framework with its own BAdIs. The BAdI names are easy to find. What they actually do with your code is not, so I read it in two lab systems: S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755) and S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758). Here is what I found, with the place in the code so you can check it in your system.

The path from VA05 to your BAdI

LayerObject
TransactionVA05 calls report SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_VIEW, application id VA05NN
Screen and ALVCL_SDOC_VIEW
Selection criteria to queryCL_SDOC_SELECT_REPORT_ADAPTER
Calls the customer BAdIsCL_SDOC_WRAPPER
The SELECT itselfCL_SDOC_SELECT_VAX5_HDB (or _ANYDB), chosen by BAdI BADI_SDOC_WRAPPER_SELECT

The same framework serves the application ids VA05NN, VA15NN, VA25NN, VA45NN and SDO1NN (see CL_BADI_SDOC_SELECT_HDB). Your implementation gets IV_APPLICATION_ID, so check it if you only want VA05.

Which BAdI does what

BAdIMethodsUse it for
BADI_SDOC_WRAPPERADAPT_RESULT_COMP, POST_PROCESSINGadd columns, fill them row by row, drop rows
BADI_SDOC_WRAPPER_MASSPOST_PROCESSING_MASSfill columns for many rows at once (one SELECT instead of one per row)
BADI_SDOC_VIEW_CUSTOM_FUNCDEFINE_CUSTOM_FUNCTION, DO_CUSTOM_FUNCTIONyour own buttons on the list
BADI_SDOC_WRAPPER_SELECTGET_SELECT_INSTANCESAP's own: two SAP implementations pick the HANA or the AnyDB select class
BADI_SDOC_SELECT_OSQLPRESELECTION, ADAPT_RESULT_COMP, POST_PROCESSING...not on the VA05 path (see point 6)

1. A column is one line in CT_RESULT_COMP, and the TABLE field decides where the value comes from

In ADAPT_RESULT_COMP you add a line to CT_RESULT_COMP. CL_SDOC_SELECT_BASIC, method SET_RESULT_COMP, types each column with cl_abap_elemdescr=>describe_by_name( ):

  • TABLE and FIELD filled (for example VBAK and your append field): the type is TABLE-FIELD and the standard SELECT reads the value from the database. You write no SELECT.
  • TABLE empty: FIELD is only the name of a data element that gives the type. The value is yours to fill in POST_PROCESSING.

The same method drops a column whose NAME already exists, without any message. SAP's columns are added before yours, so a column with a standard name simply never shows up. Use a ZZ prefix.

2. Only the visible columns are read

CL_SDOC_VIEW sends only the visible columns to the query: in START_OF_SELECTION it reads the saved ALV layout (the columns without NO_OUT), and in REFRESH_ALV_TABLE it takes the visible columns of the list. In CL_SDOC_SELECT_BASIC, method SET_RESULT_COMP_REQUIRED, each requested column goes to IT_FIELD_SEL (read from the database) or to IT_FIELD_CAL (computed, no TABLE). Everything else is not read at all.

Three consequences:

  • With no saved layout, VA05 uses a fixed basic field list and hides every other column (method HANDLE_COLUMN_VISIBILTY). Your new column exists, but starts hidden: add it to a layout.
  • In POST_PROCESSING, check IT_FIELD_CAL before you do something expensive. If the user hides your column, you don't need to compute it.
  • If your computed column needs a field the user may hide (ERDAT, KUNNR...), put it in REQUIRED_COMP. The framework then reads it anyway. SAP does the same for its own text columns: the delivery block text requires LIFSK.

3. The release difference: hidden columns with a filter

In 2020 (755), START_OF_SELECTION and REFRESH_ALV_TABLE take only the visible columns. In 2023 (758) both also take hidden columns that have an ALV filter on them. So on 2020 a hidden column with a filter is not sent to the query at all (I did not test what the filter then shows). 2023 also adds a warning when the result is cut by the maximum number of hits (message SDOC_REPORTING 011, "The number of result lines is limited to &1").

4. Dropping rows is safe for "maximum hits", and MASS runs per batch

Setting CV_IGNORE_RESULT = abap_true in POST_PROCESSING deletes the row. I first expected the list to come back shorter than the maximum hits. It does not: CL_SDOC_WRAPPER, method QUERY, keeps calling GET_NEXT until it has enough rows or there are no more.

The side effect: POST_PROCESSING_MASS is called inside that loop, so it runs once per batch, not once for the whole list. Don't count on seeing all rows in one call.

The order for each row is: the standard post-processing, then SAP's internal BAdI (BADI_SDOC_WRAPPER_INT), then yours. After the loop, the internal MASS BAdI runs first, then yours.

5. Two implementations and none of them runs, without any message

All the customer BAdIs above are single use: BADI_MAIN-SINGLE_USE = 'X' in both systems. CL_SDOC_WRAPPER (and CL_SDOC_VIEW, for the buttons BAdI) get them in the CLASS_CONSTRUCTOR like this:

try.
    get badi so_badi.
  catch cx_badi.                                    "#EC NO_HANDLER
endtry.

With two active implementations, GET BADI raises CX_BADI_MULTIPLY_IMPLEMENTED (ABAP keyword documentation of GET BADI, a subclass of CX_BADI). The empty CATCH hides it, SO_BADI stays initial and VA05 runs without any of the implementations. There is no dump and no message.

So before you create an implementation, look for the one that already exists (SE18, or table BADI_IMPL with BADI_NAME = 'BADI_SDOC_WRAPPER') and extend it. The other way out is a conflict-resolving enhancement implementation, which the same documentation describes.

6. BADI_SDOC_SELECT_OSQL is not called by VA05

It has methods with the same names (ADAPT_RESULT_COMP, POST_PROCESSING), so it looks like the right one. But the VA05 select classes CL_SDOC_SELECT_VAX5_HDB and _ANYDB inherit from CL_SDOC_SELECT_BASIC, which has no BAdI call. BADI_SDOC_SELECT_OSQL is called by CL_SDOC_SELECT_OSQL_BASIC. In my 2023 system its subclasses are the price list selections (CL_PIQ_SDPRICELIST_SELECT_CUST, _MAT) and CL_VBAK_DAAG_SELECT, not VA05.

A minimal implementation

One computed column with the age of the order in days. It needs ERDAT, so ERDAT goes to REQUIRED_COMP:

METHOD if_badi_sdoc_wrapper~adapt_result_comp.
  CHECK iv_application_id = if_sdoc_select=>co_application_id-va05nn.
  " computed column: no TABLE, FIELD is only the data element that gives the type
  " REQUIRED_COMP makes the framework read ERDAT even if the user hides that column
  INSERT VALUE #( name          = 'ZZ_AGE_DAYS'
                  field         = 'INT4'
                  text          = 'Age in days'
                  required_comp = VALUE #( ( 'ERDAT' ) ) ) INTO TABLE ct_result_comp.
  " database column: TABLE + FIELD, read by the standard SELECT
  " INSERT VALUE #( name = 'ZZ_MYFIELD' table = 'VBAK' field = 'ZZ_MYFIELD' ) INTO TABLE ct_result_comp.
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD if_badi_sdoc_wrapper~post_processing.
  " only work when the column is visible (or required by another one)
  CHECK line_exists( it_field_cal[ table_line = 'ZZ_AGE_DAYS' ] ).
  ASSIGN COMPONENT 'ERDAT' OF STRUCTURE cs_result TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<erdat>).
  ASSIGN COMPONENT 'ZZ_AGE_DAYS' OF STRUCTURE cs_result TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<age>).
  IF <erdat> IS ASSIGNED AND <age> IS ASSIGNED AND <erdat> IS NOT INITIAL.
    <age> = sy-datum - <erdat>.
  ENDIF.
ENDMETHOD.

What I did and did not test

Everything above comes from reading the code and the BAdI tables (BADI_MAIN, BADI_IMPL) in both systems. The two methods passed the syntax check in both systems, inside a local class that implements IF_BADI_SDOC_WRAPPER, and a misspelled parameter made the same check fail. I did not create a real enhancement implementation and did not run VA05 with it, so the column on the screen is not shown here. The selection screen side (your own select options) is another topic: report SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_VIEW has enhancement points of spot ES_SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_VIEW for it, and I did not go into them.

If you have VA05 in a different release and see something else, tell me in the comments.

entry.title: 10 ABAP Performance Anti-Patterns That Still Matter in SAP S/4HANA
entry.content:
10 ABAP Performance Anti-Patterns That Still Matter in SAP S/4HANA

Introduction

SAP HANA has fundamentally changed how we approach data-intensive ABAP applications. However, moving an application from SAP ECC to SAP S/4HANA does not automatically make every custom program efficient.

Database round trips, unnecessary data transfers, inefficient internal table access, and poor SQL design can still affect application performance.

A useful principle for ABAP performance engineering is:

Measure the workload first, identify the bottleneck, and optimize the operation that contributes most to execution time.

This article examines ten common ABAP performance anti-patterns, explains why they matter, and discusses practical alternatives.

The examples use illustrative custom tables and modern ABAP syntax. They should be adapted to the relevant ABAP release and validated against actual system workloads.

1. SELECT Inside LOOP: Repeated Database Access

Consider an application that retrieves sales order information and then reads a related custom status record separately for each order.

Potentially inefficient approach:

LOOP AT lt_orders INTO DATA(ls_order).

  SELECT SINGLE status
    FROM zsales_status
    WHERE vbeln = @ls_order-vbeln
    INTO @DATA(lv_status).

ENDLOOP.

The database statement can execute once for every order. For a large result set, repeated database calls may become expensive.

Alternative using a bulk read:

IF lt_orders IS NOT INITIAL.

  SELECT vbeln, status
    FROM zsales_status
    FOR ALL ENTRIES IN @lt_orders
    WHERE vbeln = @lt_orders-vbeln
    INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_status).

ENDIF.

For predictable access, store the retrieved records in a suitable hashed or sorted internal table.

Architect's note: Do not replace every SELECT inside a loop mechanically. First check the SQL trace, buffering behavior, number of calls, data volume and whether a JOIN or an internal-table data source would be more appropriate.

2. FOR ALL ENTRIES Without an Empty-Table Check

FOR ALL ENTRIES remains useful in various ABAP applications, but it requires careful handling.

Risky approach:

SELECT vbeln, status
  FROM zsales_status
  FOR ALL ENTRIES IN @lt_orders
  WHERE vbeln = @lt_orders-vbeln
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_result).

If the driving table is empty, the statement can ignore the WHERE condition and retrieve substantially more data than intended.

Safer approach:

IF lt_orders IS NOT INITIAL.

  SELECT vbeln, status
    FROM zsales_status
    FOR ALL ENTRIES IN @lt_orders
    WHERE vbeln = @lt_orders-vbeln
    INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_result).

ENDIF.

Additional considerations:

  • Remove unnecessary duplicate driving keys.

  • Retrieve only the fields needed.

  • Evaluate the resulting SQL in ST05.

  • Compare alternatives rather than assuming one syntax is always faster.

3. Reading Too Many Columns with SELECT *

Retrieving columns that an application never uses increases the amount of data transferred and processed.

Potentially inefficient:

SELECT *
  FROM zsales_header
  WHERE erdat >= @lv_date
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_headers).

More selective:

SELECT vbeln, erdat, auart
  FROM zsales_header
  WHERE erdat >= @lv_date
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_headers).

Projection matters particularly when reading wide tables or processing large result sets.

However, SELECT * is not inherently incorrect. It may be reasonable where all fields are needed and the workload is small.

The goal is to minimize unnecessary data movement without making maintainability worse.

4. Choosing the Wrong Internal Table Type

Internal table access patterns can have a measurable effect on ABAP runtime.

Consider repeatedly locating individual sales orders.

A standard table used with a linear search may become expensive as its number of rows increases.

Alternative for unique-key lookup:

DATA lt_orders TYPE HASHED TABLE OF
     ty_order
     WITH UNIQUE KEY vbeln.

READ TABLE lt_orders
  WITH TABLE KEY vbeln = lv_vbeln
  INTO DATA(ls_order).

Choosing the right table category:

Table type Typical use

StandardSequential processing and general-purpose collections
SortedOrdered access, sorted key access and ranges
HashedFrequent exact-key lookups using a complete unique key

Secondary table keys may also be useful where the same internal table is accessed through different key combinations.

The selection should reflect actual access frequency, insertion costs and memory requirements.

5. Nested Loops with Large Internal Tables

Nested loops are not automatically bad, but repeated comparisons across large collections can create significant CPU costs.

For example:

LOOP AT lt_headers INTO DATA(ls_header).

  LOOP AT lt_items INTO DATA(ls_item)
    WHERE vbeln = ls_header-vbeln.

    " Process related item

  ENDLOOP.

ENDLOOP.

With standard tables and no suitable access key, this may require extensive repeated searching.

Potential improvements include:

  • Using a sorted or hashed secondary key on the item table.

  • Using keyed internal table access.

  • Combining related records through an appropriate SQL JOIN.

  • Reducing repeated calculations inside the inner loop.

The most suitable option depends on table categories, key definitions and the number of header and item records.

6. Transferring Excessive Data to the Application Server

Not every operation needs to process all records in ABAP memory.

For example, if the only requirement is to calculate a total, transferring every matching database record may be unnecessary.

Application-side aggregation:

SELECT netwr
  FROM zsales_header
  WHERE erdat >= @lv_date
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_values).

LOOP AT lt_values INTO DATA(ls_value).
  lv_total = lv_total + ls_value-netwr.
ENDLOOP.

Database-side aggregation:

SELECT SUM( netwr )
  FROM zsales_header
  WHERE erdat >= @lv_date
  INTO @lv_total.

When the business requirement and data semantics permit it, database-side aggregation reduces data transfer and application-side processing.

For SAP HANA applications, this reflects the broader principle of code pushdown.

However, aggregation logic must preserve the correct currency, unit, filtering and business semantics.

7. Missing or Ineffective WHERE Conditions

An efficient query begins with a clearly defined data requirement.

Suppose the application needs only a particular date range and document type.

SELECT vbeln, erdat, auart
  FROM zsales_header
  WHERE erdat BETWEEN @lv_from AND @lv_to
    AND auart = @lv_auart
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_orders).

Restricting the retrieved data as early as possible is generally preferable to selecting a large dataset and filtering it afterward.

For performance-critical statements, inspect:

  • Selectivity of the filter

  • Actual execution plan

  • Cardinality and data distribution

  • Available indexes

  • Execution frequency

On SAP HANA, do not assume that adding another secondary index is automatically beneficial. Index design needs evidence and must account for maintenance overhead.

8. Treating CDS Views as Automatically Faster

Core Data Services provide powerful modelling capabilities, but merely converting an Open SQL statement to CDS does not guarantee better performance.

A CDS model with unnecessary joins, expensive calculations or excessive associations can still create a costly database workload.

Evaluate:

  • The number of records being processed.

  • Whether filters are pushed down effectively.

  • The joins generated by the model.

  • Calculations that affect execution plans.

  • Whether all projected fields and associations are required.

Practical principle: Use CDS for the right data-modelling and consumption requirements, not simply as a performance shortcut.

9. Ignoring ST05 and SAT Until Production

Performance tuning based entirely on assumptions can lead to unnecessary changes or even regressions.

Two important tools are:

ST05 — SQL Trace

Useful for investigating database-related behavior, including frequently executed SQL statements, database access patterns and execution times.

SAT — ABAP Runtime Analysis

Useful for identifying expensive ABAP processing, method calls and execution paths.

A practical investigation sequence is:

  1. Reproduce the slow transaction or report.

  2. Capture a representative baseline.

  3. Determine whether the dominant cost is in database execution, ABAP processing or another dependency.

  4. Inspect the most expensive operations.

  5. Implement one targeted change.

  6. Repeat the measurement under comparable conditions.

For more extensive SQL workload analysis, SQL Monitor can also help identify frequently executed or expensive SQL operations.

10. Optimizing Without Measuring the Result

One of the most common mistakes is assuming that a syntactic improvement necessarily delivers an application-level performance improvement.

A change from a standard internal table to a hashed table may improve repeated exact-key lookups, but it can introduce additional memory or insertion overhead.

A SQL JOIN may reduce round trips, but a poorly designed join can also create a larger intermediate result.

For each optimization, capture the evidence.

Measurement Before After

End-to-end runtimeRecord resultRecord result
SQL execution countRecord resultRecord result
Database execution timeRecord resultRecord result
Rows transferredRecord resultRecord result
ABAP processing timeRecord resultRecord result

Do not claim a percentage improvement without a reproducible measurement.

A Practical Performance Review Checklist

Before approving performance-sensitive ABAP code, I recommend checking the following:

  • Are database reads executed repeatedly inside loops?

  • Are FOR ALL ENTRIES driving tables checked for emptiness?

  • Are only required columns retrieved?

  • Are WHERE conditions restrictive enough?

  • Do internal table types match their access patterns?

  • Are nested loops using efficient keys?

  • Can appropriate aggregations execute on the database?

  • Have complex CDS statements been evaluated?

  • Have ST05 and SAT been used when performance is critical?

  • Is there measurable evidence that the proposed optimization helps?

Final Thoughts

Modern ABAP performance engineering is not about replacing every traditional statement with a newer syntax.

It is about understanding data access, system architecture, runtime behavior and the actual business workload.

Good performance decisions require three things:

Correctness, evidence and maintainability.

A change is genuinely valuable when it preserves the business result, performs better under representative conditions and remains understandable to the next developer.

Discussion

Which ABAP performance issue have you encountered most frequently in SAP S/4HANA projects?

Is it repeated database access, inefficient internal table handling, complex CDS views or something else?

I would be interested in learning how other developers investigate and resolve these bottlenecks.

Further reading

SAP Help Portal — ABAP Performance and Tuning

https://help.sap.com/docs/SUPPORT_CONTENT/abap/3353523595.html

SAP Help Portal — FOR ALL ENTRIES

https://help.sap.com/docs/SUPPORT_CONTENT/abap/3353526117.html

entry.title: Custom field in the BP credit segment (UKM000): why it shows on the screen and is never saved
entry.content:
A question in the Q&A this month shows a pattern I have seen in projects more than once. You add a field to the credit segment data of the business partner (role UKM000, table UKMBP_CMS_SGM) with BDT. The field shows on the screen, your PAI module gets the value, and after Save the value is gone. UKM_BUPA_UKMBP_CMS_SGM_GET returns it empty.

I read the standard code in two lab systems, S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755) and S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758), to see where the value gets lost. There are two separate traps, and both are in how the standard code moves the data, not in the BDT customizing.

How the standard credit segment screen moves the data

StepWhereWhat the code does
PBOUKM_BUPA_PBO_UKM200, form DIALOG_READ_SEGMENT_DATAreads the segment from the account object (CL_UKM_ACCOUNT->GET_BP_CMS_SGM) into the global work area UKMBP_CMS_SGM of function group UKM_BUPA_01
PAIUKM_BUPA_PAI_UKM200MOVE-CORRESPONDING from that work area into a structure TYPE UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM, then GO_ACCOUNT->SET_BP_CMS_SGM
Anything changed?event XCHNG, UKM_BUPA_EVENT_XCHNGasks CL_UKM_BUPA_FACTORY->WAS_ANYTHING_CHANGED; the account compares its whole UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM with the database version
Saveevent DSAVE, UKM_BUPA_EVENT_DSAVE, then CL_UKM_FACADE->SAVE_ALL and CL_UKM_BUPA_FACTORY->SAVE_ALLUKM_DB_UKMBP_CMS_EXECUTE builds the rows with MOVE-CORRESPONDING and runs UPDATE ukmbp_cms_sgm FROM TABLE

Look at the type in every step: it is UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM, never the table UKMBP_CMS_SGM.

Trap 1: the append is on the table, not on the structure

The table UKMBP_CMS_SGM is CLIENT, PARTNER, CREDIT_SGMNT and .INCLUDE UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM. If you append your field to the table itself, it is not part of UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM, and then:

  • PAI: the MOVE-CORRESPONDING into UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM drops it, so the account object never gets it.
  • Read: the account reads the segment into UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM, so PBO shows it blank and UKM_BUPA_UKMBP_CMS_SGM_GET returns it blank. That is exactly the symptom in the question.
  • Save: UKM_DB_UKMBP_CMS_EXECUTE fills the table row by MOVE-CORRESPONDING from UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM_UPD and runs UPDATE ... FROM TABLE. Your column is initial in that row, so every save of the segment writes it blank. Even if you fill it with your own UPDATE, the next standard save clears it again.

Where the field has to go:

ReleasePut the field here
S/4HANA 2020an append on the structure UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM (enhancement category "can be enhanced")
S/4HANA 2023the extension include UKM_BP_CMS_SGM_INCL_EEW_PS, which already sits inside UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM. It is the persistence include of business context UKM_BP_MD_SEGMENT (table CFD_W_BUS_CTXT), so a field from the Custom Fields app lands there too

In the 2020 lab that include and that business context do not exist; in 2023 they do. It is the only release difference I found in this chain: PAI UKM200 is identical in both, and so is the segment part of UKM_DB_UKMBP_CMS_EXECUTE.

A quick test for trap 1: write ls_sgm-zz_risk_class with ls_sgm TYPE ukm_s_bp_cms_sgm. If the syntax check says "The data object LS_SGM does not have a component called ZZ_RISK_CLASS", your field is on the table, not on the structure. I got exactly that message in my negative control.

Trap 2: your screen field lives in your own function group

BDT calls the PBO and PAI modules of your view inside your function group. Your screen work area (TABLES ukmbp_cms_sgm, or whatever you use) is a different memory area from the one in UKM_BUPA_01, and the standard PAI saves its own. There is no *_COLLECT module for this view.

What both function groups share is the account object:

  • CL_UKM_FACADE=>CREATE keeps the facade in the static attribute XO_FACADE and creates it only once.
  • CL_UKM_BUPA_FACTORY->GET_CREDIT_ACCOUNT keeps the accounts in the internal table _T_ACC_OBJS, by partner and segment.

Your function group runs in the same internal session as UKM_BUPA_01 during BP, so you get the same object the standard uses. Set your field on it and the rest is standard:

  • XCHNG sees the change, because GET_CHANGES in CL_UKM_ACCOUNT compares the whole structure (IF _s_bp_cms_sgm_db <> _s_bp_cms_sgm). BP does not answer "no changes".
  • DSAVE writes it. You do not need your own XCHNG or DSAVE for this field.

The PAI order decides who wins

The standard PAI of UKM200 copies its whole work area into the account, and that work area still holds the PBO value of your field. If it runs after your PAI, it writes the old value back.

The order is in form FUNCTION_PAI_CALL of SAPLBUSS (the BDT): sections in the order of their position on the screen (TBZ3I-POSNR), and inside a section, the views by position (TBZ3H-POSNR). In both labs view UKM200 sits in section UKM200 at position 0100000. So place your view after it: in the same section with a higher position, or in a section below it.

Minimal code for your view

" Function group of your view. Screen field: UKMBP_CMS_SGM-ZZ_RISK_CLASS
" (TABLES ukmbp_cms_sgm in the TOP include). The field is in UKM_S_BP_CMS_SGM.

FORM get_account CHANGING co_account TYPE REF TO cl_ukm_account.
  DATA ls_but000 TYPE but000.
  DATA ls_std    TYPE ukmbp_cms_sgm.

  CLEAR co_account.
  CALL FUNCTION 'BUP_BUPA_BUT000_GET'
    IMPORTING
      e_but000 = ls_but000.
  " the segment selected on the standard screen
  CALL FUNCTION 'UKM_BUPA_UKMBP_CMS_SGM_GET'
    IMPORTING
      e_ukmbp_cms_sgm = ls_std.
  CHECK ls_but000-partner IS NOT INITIAL AND ls_std-credit_sgmnt IS NOT INITIAL.
  " same singleton as the standard view, so the same account object
  co_account = cl_ukm_facade=>create( i_activity = cl_ukm_cnst_eventing=>bp_maintenance
                 )->get_bupa_factory( )->get_credit_account( i_partner      = ls_but000-partner
                                                             i_credit_sgmnt = ls_std-credit_sgmnt ).
ENDFORM.

FUNCTION z_ukm_pbo_zukm01.    " PBO module of your view
  DATA lo_account TYPE REF TO cl_ukm_account.
  DATA ls_sgm     TYPE ukm_s_bp_cms_sgm.

  PERFORM get_account CHANGING lo_account.
  CHECK lo_account IS BOUND.
  lo_account->get_bp_cms_sgm( EXPORTING i_check_validity = space
                              IMPORTING es_bp_cms_sgm    = ls_sgm ).
  ukmbp_cms_sgm-zz_risk_class = ls_sgm-zz_risk_class.
ENDFUNCTION.

FUNCTION z_ukm_pai_zukm01.    " PAI module of your view
  DATA lo_account TYPE REF TO cl_ukm_account.
  DATA ls_sgm     TYPE ukm_s_bp_cms_sgm.
  DATA lv_aktyp   TYPE tbz0k-aktyp.

  CALL FUNCTION 'BUS_PARAMETERS_ISSTA_GET'
    IMPORTING
      e_aktyp = lv_aktyp.
  CHECK lv_aktyp <> '03'.     " 03 = display, same constant the standard uses
  PERFORM get_account CHANGING lo_account.
  CHECK lo_account IS BOUND.
  lo_account->get_bp_cms_sgm( EXPORTING i_check_validity = space
                              IMPORTING es_bp_cms_sgm    = ls_sgm ).
  IF ls_sgm-zz_risk_class <> ukmbp_cms_sgm-zz_risk_class.
    ls_sgm-zz_risk_class = ukmbp_cms_sgm-zz_risk_class.
    lo_account->set_bp_cms_sgm( is_bp_cms_sgm = ls_sgm ).
  ENDIF.
ENDFUNCTION.

The PBO reads from the account and not from the database, so after a PAI round trip the screen shows what is really going to be saved.

What I tested, and what I did not

  • Read in both labs: PBO and PAI of UKM200, the events XCHNG, DSAVE and DSAVB, CL_UKM_FACADE, CL_UKM_BUPA_FACTORY, CL_UKM_ACCOUNT, UKM_DB_UKMBP_CMS_EXECUTE and the BDT form FUNCTION_PAI_CALL.
  • Syntax check: the code above passed in 2020 and in 2023, written as forms in a report, with the standard field CUST_GROUP in place of ZZ_RISK_CLASS, because the labs do not have the custom field. With ZZ_RISK_CLASS it fails with the message from trap 1, as expected.
  • Not tested: a real BDT view on the BP screen and a real save. I did not create the field, the view or a business partner. For the Custom Fields app I only saw the business context in the table; I did not check which UIs it offers for this context.

If your system behaves differently, tell me in the comments with the release, and I will compare.

entry.title: Two calls, one sales order: what BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE locks and why the second fails at once
entry.content:
Two iFlows send a change for the same sales order a few seconds apart, and the second one comes back with:

V1 042: Sales document &1 is currently being processed by &2.

The usual reactions are "add a wait in the iFlow" or "it is a CPI problem". It is neither. The behavior is in the standard lock code of the sales document, and once you see it, the fix on the interface side is clear. I read it in two lab systems, S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755) and S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758).

Where the BAPI takes the lock

StepObject
1BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE calls SD_SALESDOCUMENT_CHANGE
2step "08. read the salesdocument": SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_READ
3form BELEG_LESEN of SAPMV45A, then form VBAK_SELECT (include MV45AFDB_VBAK_SELECT)
4form BELEG_SPERREN (include MV45AF0B_BELEG_SPERREN)
5SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_ENQUEUE, then ENQUEUE_EVVBAKE

Three things come out of this chain:

  • The lock is taken when the order is read, before your changes are even looked at. A call that would change nothing still collides.
  • The whole document is locked. Lock object EVVBAKE has one table, VBAK, with key MANDT + VBELN, mode E. Header and all items are one lock. Two calls that change different items of the same order still collide. The form comment says it directly: "Der Beleg wird komplett und exklusiv gesperrt" (the document is locked completely and exclusively).
  • It is the only door. The where-used list of SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_ENQUEUE has one caller in the standard: BELEG_SPERREN.

Why the second call does not wait

SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_ENQUEUE has _wait with default space, and BELEG_SPERREN does not pass it. So ENQUEUE_EVVBAKE fails at once when someone else holds the lock, and BELEG_SPERREN raises E 042.

There is a retry loop in BELEG_SPERREN, 10 times WAIT UP TO 1 SECONDS, but only for two cases: a call from CRM with a reference document, and the assembly processing (call_activity eq activity_assembly). A BAPI call from an interface is neither, so it gets no retry from the standard.

The &2 in the message is the user who holds the lock (BELEG_SPERREN takes it from SY-MSGV1 of the enqueue). If &2 is your own interface user, your own messages are colliding with each other.

I ran it in the 2023 lab with a small console class in $TMP. Session A took EVVBAKE for one order and kept it. Session B, a second session through RFC destination NONE, called BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE for the same order. It came back in 0.09 seconds with E V1 042, and &2 was my own user, because both sessions ran under it. After session A released the lock, the same call from session B went through.

One thing I learned on the way: a call with SIMULATION = 'X' does not leave the order locked. In simulation mode SD_SALES_DOCU_MAINTAIN ends with SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_INIT, and right after a simulation call ENQUEUE_READ showed no lock on VBAK. So you cannot reproduce V1 042 with two simulation calls, and a simulation check before the real call does not block it.

How long the lock lives

SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_ENQUEUE has _scope with default '2'. With scope 2 the lock goes to the update task at COMMIT WORK, and the update releases it when it ends (SAP Help, Function Modules for Lock Requests: https://help.sap.com/docs/ABAP_PLATFORM_NEW/ec1c9c8191b74de98feb94001a95dd76/cf21eebf446011d189700000e8322d00.html).

So after a successful change the order stays locked until the update finishes, not until your call returns. In BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT:

  • WAIT blank: COMMIT WORK. Your session goes on while the update still holds the lock, so the next call for the same order can hit V1 042.
  • WAIT = 'X': COMMIT WORK AND WAIT. It returns after the update, and the lock is gone.

When the BAPI ends with an error and BEHAVE_WHEN_ERROR is left blank (the default), SD_SALESDOCUMENT_CHANGE releases the lock itself before it returns (BELEG_ENTSPERREN in step 13), so a failed call does not keep the order locked.

What to do on the interface side

  1. Serialize by order number. Two messages for the same order should never run at the same time. In the middleware this means one sequence per sales order (or one message at a time for the same order), not just a global retry.
  2. Treat V1 042 as "try again later", not as a data error. Check RETURN for TYPE E, ID V1, NUMBER 042, roll back, wait a bit and call again. Any other error is a real error.
  3. Commit with WAIT = 'X' when the next call in the same session touches the same order.
  4. Read &2. Your own technical user means parallel messages of your own; a dialog user means someone is in VA02.

If the caller is ABAP (an RFC wrapper, a custom inbound), the retry looks like this:

DATA lv_vbeln  TYPE vbeln_va.
DATA ls_header TYPE bapisdh1.
DATA ls_inx    TYPE bapisdh1x.
DATA lt_return TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF bapiret2 WITH EMPTY KEY.

ls_inx-updateflag = 'U'.
DO 5 TIMES.
  CLEAR lt_return.
  CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
    EXPORTING
      salesdocument    = lv_vbeln
      order_header_in  = ls_header
      order_header_inx = ls_inx
    TABLES
      return           = lt_return.
  " V1 042: the order is locked by someone else, the BAPI did not wait
  IF NOT line_exists( lt_return[ type = 'E' id = 'V1' number = '042' ] ).
    EXIT.
  ENDIF.
  CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
  WAIT UP TO 2 SECONDS.
ENDDO.

IF line_exists( lt_return[ type = 'E' ] ) OR line_exists( lt_return[ type = 'A' ] ).
  CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
ELSE.
  " WAIT = X: COMMIT WORK AND WAIT, the update ends before the next call
  CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
    EXPORTING
      wait = abap_true.
ENDIF.

Five tries and two seconds are just an example; size them by how long your updates take.

2020 and 2023

The lock itself is the same in both: EVVBAKE, mode E, _scope '2', _wait blank, and the same retry condition. The 2023 BELEG_SPERREN has one more step after EVVBAKE, a call to REQUEST_VCM_LOCKS (class CL_SD_SLS_VCM_FACTORY), which the 2020 code does not have. It does not change anything above.

What I tested, and what I did not

  • Read in both labs: BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE, SD_SALESDOCUMENT_CHANGE, SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_READ, the forms BELEG_LESEN, VBAK_SELECT and BELEG_SPERREN, SD_SALES_DOCUMENT_ENQUEUE, BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT, the lock object EVVBAKE (DD27S) and the message text in T100.
  • Syntax check: the retry code passed in 2020 and 2023. A negative control (a wrong component name in the table expression) failed as expected.
  • Run in the 2023 lab: the collision above, with one session holding EVVBAKE and the BAPI called from a second session, and the simulation call that leaves no lock. Nothing was saved: the BAPI calls ran with SIMULATION = 'X', and the test class was deleted afterwards.
  • Not tested: two interfaces under real load, the time the update keeps the lock after a real COMMIT, and any middleware configuration. The scope 2 behavior is from the SAP documentation above, not from a measurement of mine.

If you see V1 042 even with serialized calls, tell me which user shows in &2 and I will take a look.

entry.title: VF04 does not show my document: six checks in the code
entry.content:
"VF04 does not show my document" comes up again and again in the forum, and the answers usually go straight to the copy control or the billing type. Most of the time the reason is earlier and simpler. VF04 (report SDBILLDL) does not read VBAK or LIKP. It reads one table, VKDFS, the billing index, through RV_READ_INVOICE_INDEX. So a document shows only if:

  1. it has a VKDFS row, and
  2. neither the selection screen nor your authorizations filter that row out.

Both parts are in the code, and I read them in two lab systems, S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755) and S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758). The logic below is the same in both.

First check, always: SE16 on VKDFS with VBELN = your order or delivery. No row means reason 1. A row means reasons 2 to 6.

1. The document never got a VKDFS row

The index is written when the document is saved, in function group V05I:

VKDFS-FKTYPWritten whenForm in V05I
A, order-related (B when VBAK-KNUMA is filled)item billing status VBUP-FKSAA is A or B; billing plan items by their billing plan datesAP_01, INDEX_VKDFS_AUFBAUEN
L, delivery-relatedheader billing status FKSTK is A or B and goods movement status WBSTK is blank or CLK_01, INDEX_VKDFS_AUFBAUEN_LIEFERUNG
I, intercompanyFKIVK is A or B, and FKSTK is C (or blank with WBSTK blank or C)LK_01, INDEX_VKDFS_AUFBAUEN_LIEF_IV

The one that catches people: a delivery without goods issue (WBSTK = A or B) has no row at all, so no selection in VF04 will ever find it. Post the goods issue first.

Two more things on this side:

  • Customer exits. Enhancement V05I0001 has EXIT_SAPLV05I_001 (orders), _002 (deliveries) and _003 (intercompany). In the code, an exit that returns '0' suppresses the row and '1' forces it. If something is active in CMOD there, look at it first.
  • The row is missing but the status is right. This can happen, for example, after an update that failed halfway. The standard report RVV05IVB ("Reorganization of sales document indices") rebuilds the billing index for sales documents, deliveries and billing documents.

2. "Billing date to" is today

PARAMETERS: p_fkdab LIKE vbco7-fkdat_bis DEFAULT sy-datlo.

The read uses FKDAT between "from" and "to". A billing date in the future is not listed until you change the "to" date. For billing plan items, VKDFS-FKDAT is the billing plan date (FPLT-AFDAT), not the order date.

3. Only "Deliveries" is ticked by default

In AT SELECTION-SCREEN OUTPUT, when no checkbox is set and the user parameter VF04_SEL is not set, the code ticks only P_ALLEL:

p_allel = gc_charx.

So order-related rows (FKTYP A), rebate (B), intercompany (I) and billing document requests (X) are not selected. Debit and credit memo requests, or services billed order-related, do not show until you tick "Order-Related".

The user parameter VF04_SEL (SU3) presets the boxes, one character per box, in this order:

PositionBox
1Order-Related
2Deliveries
3Rebate-Related
4Intercompany billing
5No Document with Billing Block
6Documents with POD Status
7Billing Document Requests

X means ticked; O, 0, a dot or a blank means not ticked. Any other character gives warning VF 420 and the parameter is ignored. Example: XX.X ticks order-related, deliveries and intercompany.

4. "No Document with Billing Block" only hides blocks assigned to the billing type

VKDFS stores the billing block (FAKSK). Without the tick, blocked documents are listed, and the billing run then stops on the block. With the tick, form AUSDUENNEN_XVKDFS in V05H removes a row only when the pair billing block and billing type exists in TVFSP. That is the assignment in SPRO "Define Blocking Reasons for Billing" (view V_TVFSP). A block that is not assigned to the billing type does not hide the document.

In the 2023 lab: VKDFS has 156 rows (70 order-related, 56 delivery-related, 30 intercompany). 68 of them have block 08 "Check Credit Memo" on billing type RE, and 08/RE is in TVFSP, so the tick hides those 68.

5. Intercompany rows carry other values

For FKTYP I, form INDEX_VKDFS_AUFBAUEN_LIEF_IV fills VKDFS from the intercompany fields of the delivery:

VKDFScomes from
VKORGLIKP-VKOIV (sales org for intercompany billing)
FKARTLIKP-FKAIV (intercompany billing type)
FKDATLIKP-FKDIV
KUNNRLIKP-KUNIV (internal customer)

A variant with the delivering sales organization, or with the customer billing type, does not find them.

6. No display authorization, no row

After the read, RV_READ_INVOICE_INDEX checks every row with activity 03: V_VBRK_FKA for the billing type and V_VBRK_VKO for the sales organization. A row that fails is deleted from the list. The only hint is the information message VB 500, "The list is incomplete due to missing authorizations", easy to miss, and in a background job it only goes to the job log. Two users with the same variant can see different lists.

Symptom and where to look

SymptomLook at
no row in VKDFSstatuses FKSTK, WBSTK, FKSAA; exits V05I0001; then RVV05IVB
row exists, not in the listthe "to" date, the ticked boxes, VF04_SEL
blocked documents appear or disappearthe tick and the V_TVFSP assignment
intercompany missingthe variant values against LIKP-VKOIV, FKAIV, FKDIV, KUNIV
another user sees it, you do notmessage VB 500, then V_VBRK_FKA and V_VBRK_VKO for your user

What I tested, and what I did not

  • Read in both labs: SDBILLDL (selection screen and defaults), RV_READ_INVOICE_INDEX in V05H (forms VKDFS_INIT, AUSDUENNEN_XVKDFS and the two authorization forms) and the index forms in V05I. Same logic in 2020 and 2023.
  • Counted in the 2023 lab: the VKDFS rows by type and by billing block, and the TVFSP entry 08/RE.
  • Not tested: I did not run VF04, set VF04_SEL in SU3, or run RVV05IVB (it writes the index). The exit behavior is from the code, not from a running exit.

If your document still does not show after these six checks, post the VKDFS row (or the fact that there is none) and the statuses, and I will take a look.

entry.title: Fluid API for Abapsmith: breaking ADT limits
entry.content:
AI agents working with SAP ABAP have always hit the wall - they can do whatever the ADT interface allows, and nothing more. Need to create a view, a transaction, or an IMG customizing entry? ADT has no endpoint for it, so the agent stops and you do it by hand.

Fluid API in Abapsmith removes that wall. When the agent lacks a tool, it creates one inside your SAP system, uses it right away, and moves on.

What it looks like in practice

You ask: "Create a BAdI spot for our pricing enhancement in package ZDEMO."

The agent creates a small utility class in the S4 system in local package, and call this new tool to create a BAdI spot. 

Why it matters
- Fewer dead ends. Work that used to need manual steps in SAP GUI (views, search helps, transport entries, IMG settings, Floorplan Manager configuration, authorization traces) can now be done by the agent.
- A clean system. Nothing is pre-installed. Small helper classes are deployed only when a task needs them. They live in one dedicated local package, $ABAPSMITH_FLUID_API, so they are easy to find and never end up in a transport.
- Controlled by design. Every action is classified as read, change or execute. Changing actions state which object, package and transport they touch, and Abapsmith checks that before anything runs. 
- Extensible. Missing something that isn't built in? Your agent can write a plugin for it using skill. The plugin then works like any built-in tool and goes through the same safety checks. 

What's included today

classic

Things ADT has no write endpoint for: views, transactions, search helps, indexes, packages, transport entries, transports of copies. Also reads transport logs and import queues.

core

Table rows, function module interfaces, SAP documentation, change documents and enqueue locks. Can also call any function module (call_fm) and run an ABAP snippet (eval). Both are off by default.

enh

Enhancement spots, BAdI definitions, filters and implementations.

img

IMG customizing: preview the rows, create the request, write the change.

fpm

Floorplan Manager configuration: find an app, read its outline, resolve it, list its events.

ui

Classic screens: fields, flow logic and function codes.

authtrace

Authorization trace: status, switch on and off, read the result, SU53.

log

Application log (SLG1) messages.

run

Run a classic report and capture its output.

scan

Search source text across a package or a set of objects.

rt

Self-test of the runtime.

Summary

The agent is no longer limited to what the ADT API offers. If a tool is missing, it builds one inside SAP, safely and on demand.

Want to know more? Please check the project itself, it is open-source:  https://github.com/Freight-Art/abapsmith

entry.title: I counted the released APIs in my S/4HANA 2023 lab. The BAPI numbers surprised me
entry.content:
"Can I use this in ABAP Cloud?"

I hear this question in almost every class. A student finds a function module in an old program, or in a forum answer from 2012, and wants to know if it still has a future.

The honest answer is always the same: open the object in ADT, go to Properties, API State, and look. It works. But it works one object at a time, and one day I wanted the whole picture. How much of the system is actually released? And how much of what we use every day is not?

So I counted. Everything below comes from table ARS_W_API_STATE in my S/4HANA 2023 lab (SAP_BASIS 758, FPS01), the table behind that API State tab.

Five contracts, one big number

A release is always for a contract. C0 is for extending (adding fields, implementing extension points). C1 is for using the object inside the system, which is what your ABAP Cloud code needs. C2 is for using it as a remote API, C3 for configuration content and C4 for AMDP.

ContractStateEntries
C0RELEASED1,241
C1RELEASED24,670
C1RELEASED_WITH_FEATURE_TOGGLE266
C1DEPRECATED461
C1NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED642
C1NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED_STABLE646
C2RELEASED4,601
C2DEPRECATED192
C2NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED_STABLE6
C3RELEASED346
C4RELEASED4

C1 is where the action is, with 24,670 released entries. And when I looked at what is released, across all contracts, most of it is data: 12,972 CDS entities, 4,104 tables and structures, 3,827 data elements. Then 3,110 interfaces, 1,444 BAdI definitions and 1,157 classes.

And function modules? 39.

What surprised me most

Thirty-nine. In a system where all of us grew up calling function modules.

Then I looked at the BAPIs. My lab has 5,487 function modules whose name starts with BAPI. Only 19 of them are released. 148 have an explicit entry saying NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED. The other 5,320 have no entry at all.

I'll admit I first read "no entry" as "not decided yet". It isn't. For ABAP Cloud, no release means no use. The 148 explicit ones are actually the lucky ones, because that entry is where SAP tells you where to go: 142 of the 148 name a successor (76 a RAP business object, 62 a CDS view, 4 a class).

Some of them you probably know:

  • BAPI_PO_CREATE1 goes to I_PURCHASEORDERTP_2 (I wrote about that move in Goodbye BAPI_PO_CREATE1?)
  • BAPI_SALESORDER_CREATEFROMDAT2 goes to I_SALESORDERTP
  • BAPI_ACC_DOCUMENT_POST goes to I_JOURNALENTRYTP
  • BAL_LOG_CREATE goes to CL_BALI_LOG

And a few surprises in the other direction. BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT and BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK are released for C1. I didn't expect the old commit pair on the released side.

BAL_LOG_MSG_ADD is NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED with no successor at all, even though BAL_LOG_CREATE points to CL_BALI_LOG. In the new API you add the items to the log object, so the successor of the family covers it, but the entry doesn't tell you that.

And CONVERSION_EXIT_ALPHA_INPUT is NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED_STABLE, also without a successor. Here the answer isn't another function, it's the language itself: |{ lv_value ALPHA = IN }|.

Ok, but what does this change in my day?

Three things, for me.

First, "no entry" is an answer. If a function module doesn't show anything in the API State, don't wait for a release. Look for the business object or the CDS view that covers the same business.

Second, the explicit NOT_TO_BE_RELEASED is good news, because it comes with directions. Before you search the internet for "replacement of BAPI_X", look at the API State. The successor is often right there.

Third, you don't need to count like I did to see the full list. SAP publishes it, with the successors, in the Cloudification Repository on GitHub (SAP/abap-atc-cr-cv-s4hc), and there is a viewer where you can search by name. But if you want the numbers of your own system, this is the query I started with:

SELECT compatibility_contract, release_state, COUNT(*) AS entries
  FROM ars_w_api_state
  GROUP BY compatibility_contract, release_state

These numbers are from one S/4HANA 2023 lab. Every release moves them, and that's kind of the point: the released side grows a little every time.

Which one surprised you? Feel free to comment, especially if you moved from a BAPI to its successor and found something the old one did that the new one doesn't.

entry.title: That number on the SAP screen may not live in any table: a WB2R_SV story
entry.content:
This week a question in the forum caught my eye. Someone needed the Net Amount that transaction WB2R_SV shows, in a Fiori Elements report. It sounds like a small request. The number is right there on the screen, so it has to be in some table, right?

Maybe yes... maybe not.

In my classes I call the method for this kind of question "press /h and dig". This time I didn't even need the debugger. Reading the report was enough, and what I found is a pattern that I think is worth more than the answer itself.

Following the number

WB2R_SV starts program RWB2R_VENDOR_SETTLEMENT (WB2R_SC is its twin for customers, with RWB2R_CUSTOMER_SETTLEMENT). The list with the Net Amount column is printed by function module WLF_PRINT_AB_HEAD, from an internal table of type KOMLFK.

That was the first clue. KOMLFK is not a table. In SE11 it is a structure, "Settlement Management: Document Header". The KOM prefix usually means a communication structure, the kind that carries data between programs while they run, like KOMK and KOMP in pricing or KOMV for the conditions.

So who fills it? In include RWB2R_REBATE_SETTLEMENTF01, FORM SETTLE_CONTRACT creates an object of class CL_WB2_REBATE_SETTLEMENT_1 and calls its method SETTLEMENT for each contract and settlement date. The method returns the settlement document as it would be created: KOMLFK for the header, KOMLFP for the items, KOMV for the conditions. The Net Amount on the screen is KOMLFK-NETWR.

In other words, before you settle, this number is not stored anywhere. The report calculates it every time you run it.

Then a detail that is the difference between a check run and a bad day: COMMIT WORK only happens when the run type is blank. Domain WB2_CCS_TESTRUN has three values: blank for the live run, X for the check run (the default on the selection screen) and S for simulation. Check run and simulation calculate everything and post nothing.

What surprised me most

WBRK, the settlement document header table, also has a field NETWR. Same data element, NETWR_LF, "Net Settlement Amount". Same currency field next to it, WAERL.

If you do a where-used on the data element, you find WBRK and you think: there it is. And it is the right field, but for a different question. WBRK has what was settled. KOMLFK has what would be settled if you ran it now. Same name, same data element, a different moment in time.

And one more. Choosing simulation doesn't only change the posting.
