When you switch the run type to simulation, FORM ADJUST_SELECTION_RUN_TYPE changes the selection for you: it clears the filter that keeps only active contracts, and excludes only the deleted and archive-ready ones. So a simulation can show contracts that a check run would not even select. Good to know before you compare two lists and wonder why they don't match.

Three questions before I promise a report

Ok, but what does this change in my day? These are the questions I ask now, before anyone hears "sure, I'll add that column".

Is the value stored or calculated? If the trail ends in a structure filled at run time, there is no field to select. KOM structures, totals built in a loop, results of a simulation: all of these live only while the program runs.

If it's calculated, who calculates it, and can I call it? Here the logic is in CL_WB2_REBATE_SETTLEMENT_1, which has no entry in ARS_W_API_STATE. Not released. You can call it from classic ABAP on-premise, for example in the query class of a custom entity, but not from ABAP Cloud. And you pay the whole settlement logic for every row, so the list needs filters.

Does the user need "what was" or "what would be"? If it is what was settled, the answer is much simpler: there is a released CDS view for settlement documents, I_SETTLMTDOC, with SupplierTotalNetAmount, CustomerTotalNetAmount and the link back to the contract and the settlement date. If it is what would be settled, you're back to calling the calculation.

In this case, asking the third question first would have saved most of the digging.

To be honest about the limits: my lab has no condition contracts (WB2_V_CAL_CONTR is empty), so I read the code, the DDIC and the release states on S/4HANA 2023, but I did not run a settlement.

Have you ever had a "small report" that turned out to be a whole calculation? Feel free to comment, I'd like to know which one it was for you.

entry.title: Business AI in ABAP Cloud - Embedding AI with the ABAP AI SDK (Part 2)
entry.content:
Business AI in ABAP Cloud - Embedding AI with the ABAP AI SDK (Part 2)

Cheers ABAP Folks!

In my last blog post, we discussed the high-level strategy for implementing business AI capabilities in ABAP Cloud. We looked at the two pillars, Embedded AI in ABAP and Agentic AI via Joule, and when to use which approach. If you haven't read it yet, I'd recommend starting there for the bigger picture.

Today, we're going hands-on. This post dives into Embedded AI, the capabilities that run directly inside your ABAP application, powered by the ABAP AI SDK. We'll walk through the fundamentals, introduce the SDK, and then look at two concrete use cases using everyone's favorite business scenario: Trip & Expense Management.

Yes, trip & expense management. We all love it, don't we? Nothing brings more joy to a business traveler than filling out expense reports after a long trip. So, let's see how AI can take some of that joy... I mean burden... away.

 

 

The Fundamentals: Connecting ABAP to AI

Before you write a single line of AI-related ABAP code, you need to get the plumbing right. All embedded AI scenarios in ABAP Cloud require a connection to SAP AI Core, specifically to the Generative AI Hub that provides access to Large Language Models (LLMs) hosted by hyperscalers.

This connection is established via Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM), a framework that allows you to manage and operate AI scenarios in a standardized, transportable way. Think of ISLM as the lifecycle backbone: it handles connectivity, model deployment, prompt management, and the runtime configuration that ties everything together.

Setting Up the Connection

The setup follows a straightforward pattern (SAP Help, Set Up ABAP AI SDK powered by ISLM)

  1. Subscribe to SAP AI Core in your SAP BTP subaccount and enable the required service plan.
  2. Create a service instance and service key for SAP AI Core in the BTP cockpit.
  3. Establish connectivity between SAP AI Core and your ABAP system by creating a communication arrangement based on communication scenario SAP_COM_0A69.

This is a customer-managed outbound integration, which means you own the connection setup. Once established, ISLM can create and activate model deployments, and the ABAP AI SDK can execute prompts against the deployed models. For a detailed step-by-step walkthrough, I recommend the tutorial Set Up SAP BTP and Integrate SAP AI Core with ISLM on SAP Developers.

The ABAP AI SDK, Your AI Toolbox

With the connection established, let's talk about the tool you'll actually use in your ABAP code: the ABAP AI SDK. It's a typed, ABAP-native reuse library that provides access to generative AI functionality via ISLM. It is available across the full ABAP Cloud landscape, covering:

  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition & On-Premise
  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
  • SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment (Steampunk)

This means the same SDK, the same APIs, the same patterns, regardless of where your ABAP system runs.

What's in for me?

The ABAP AI SDK offers a set of APIs built around common LLM usage patterns:

  • Completion API – Send a prompt to an LLM and receive a generated text response. This is the core building block for most embedded AI scenarios.
  • Prompt Library API – Work with prompt templates predefined in ISLM, including parameterized prompts with runtime variable substitution. Very useful when you want to keep your prompts maintainable and out of your ABAP code.
  • Connectivity management – The SDK handles the connection to the Generative AI Hub transparently. You reference an intelligent scenario by name, and the SDK resolves the rest.
  • Exception handling – Typed ABAP exceptions, so you can integrate AI calls into your existing error handling patterns without reinventing the wheel.

The APIs are vendor-neutral, meaning the same ABAP code works regardless of which underlying LLM provider is configured in SAP AI Core. If your organization switches from one model to another, you change the configuration in ISLM, not your ABAP code. Your CTO changes their mind about the AI vendor? No problem, no code change required – ok, to be honest with you: The prompting might be polished most probably a little.

The Simplest Possible Call

To give you a feel for the developer experience, here's the simplest possible AI call using the Completion API (SAP ABAP Cheat Sheets, Generative AI)

" Get a Completion API instance for your intelligent scenario
DATA(ai_api) = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'Z_MY_SCENARIO' ).

" Execute a prompt and get the result
DATA(result) = ai_api->execute_for_string( `Classify this trip as customer-facing or internal.` ).

" Retrieve the generated text
DATA(completion) = result->get_completion( ).

Three lines of ABAP. That's it. The factory creates an instance tied to your intelligent scenario (which contains all the connection and model details), you execute a prompt, and you get back the LLM's response as a string. No HTTP client setup, no JSON parsing, no authentication handling. The SDK takes care of all of that. If you've ever tried calling a REST API from ABAP the "old-fashioned way", you'll know exactly how much boilerplate this saves you.

Of course, real-world scenarios are a bit more involved. You'll use prompt templates with parameters, handle exceptions, and integrate the result into your business logic. But the fundamental pattern stays the same.

Orchestration Capabilities

For enterprise-grade AI scenarios, the ABAP AI SDK also supports orchestration through the SAP AI Core Orchestration Service. This adds capabilities that are critical for production use:

  • Data Masking – Automatically redact sensitive information (personal data, financial details) before it reaches the LLM. Essential for data protection and GDPR compliance, and something your compliance team will thank you for.
  • Document Grounding – Enrich your prompts with business-relevant context from documents, reducing hallucinations and improving response accuracy. Because an LLM that confidently makes things up is entertaining at dinner parties, but not in your ERP system.
  • Content Filtering – Ensure that LLM responses are safe, appropriate, and compliant with your organisation's policies.

These capabilities are configured at the orchestration level, so you don't need to implement masking or filtering logic yourself in ABAP. It's handled for you.

 

Let’s get our hands dirty: Trip & Expense Management

For the rest of this blog post, we'll use a Trip & Expense Management application as our running example. Picture a RAP-based Fiori application where employees create travel requests, and after the trip, submit expense reports.

We'll tackle two concrete use cases:

  1. Data Prediction with Fiori Input Assistance: Automatically categorizing a trip as "customer-facing" or "internal" based on the trip description.
  2. Data Extraction from files:  Extracting structured data (payment amounts, categories, etc.) from uploaded receipt documents.

Both are real-world scenarios that demonstrate different facets of the ABAP AI SDK. And both address the same fundamental truth: nobody enjoys filling out forms manually when a machine could do it better and faster. Let's start.

 

Use Case 1: Trip Categorization with RAP Recommendations

The Problem

When an employee creates a travel request, they need to fill out several fields: destination, purpose, cost center, and importantly, trip category (e.g. "customer-facing" or "internal"). This categorization drives downstream processes like approval workflows, budget allocation, and reporting. Today, users pick the category manually. They might get it wrong, or they pick whatever option is closest to the mouse cursor. What if the system could propose the right category automatically, based on the trip description?

The Solution: Fiori Input Assistance

This is exactly what Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations is designed for. RAP recommendations are a built-in input assistance feature in the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) that proposes field values for input fields on an SAP Fiori UI (SAP Help, Defining RAP Recommendations). Available since SAP BTP ABAP Environment 2602 and SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2602, RAP Recommendations can be implemented using either deterministic rules or generative AI, and you can even mix both approaches in the same application. The key principles of RAP recommendations:

  • They are exposed in SAP Fiori as a recommendation pattern of type input assistance, meaning the user sees suggested values directly in the input field.
  • They are built on top of a value help, so you need an existing value help for the target field.
  • They are triggered by side effects: when the user changes a source field (e.g. trip description), the recommendation function runs and proposes values for the target field (e.g. trip category).
  • They integrate seamlessly with the RAP programming model. No custom UI development required. Zero. Nada.

Figure 1: Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations

How It Works: The Architecture

The implementation involves three layers:

  1. Behavior Definition – Declare which fields receive recommendations and define the recommendation function.
  2. Behavior Implementation – Implement the recommendation logic in the behavior pool, using the ABAP AI SDK to call an LLM for intelligent categorization.
  3. Projection Behavior Definition – Expose the recommendations in the projection layer for the Fiori UI.

If you've built a RAP Business Object before, this will feel very familiar. It's the same layered pattern, just with AI sprinkled on top.

Step 1: Define Recommendations in the Behavior Definition

In your behavior definition, you mark the target field as relevant for recommendations, declare a recommendation function and define a side effect on which the recommendation function should be triggered. This tells the RAP framework: whenever the user changes the “title” field, execute function GetRecommendedValuesFunction and propose values for attribute “type”. The user types "Customer workshop in Berlin" and the system immediately suggests "Customer-facing". It almost feels like the system is reading the user's mind, except it's reading their input field.

define behavior for ZR_AITRIP alias Trip
{
  //Define for which fields an recommendation output is generated
  field ( recommendations ) Type;

  //Define the recommendation function itself
  recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction;

  //Define the trigger (e.g. other context field)
  side effects
  {
    recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction 
      executed on field Title;
  }
}

Step 2: Implement the Recommendation Logic

In the behavior pool, you implement the recommendation function. This is where the ABAP AI SDK comes in. You use the completion API to ask an LLM to categorize the trip based on the available context:

  1. Read the current entity data (description, destination, etc.)
  2. Build a prompt with the trip context, based on your system's master data
  3. Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API
  4. Parse the LLM response
  5. Return the recommended value(s) with scores

The recommendation function returns a list of proposed values, each with a score and a flag indicating whether it's the suggested (top-ranked) value. The Fiori UI renders these as input assistance. The user can accept, modify, or override the suggestion. The AI proposes, the human decides. As it should be.

The full implementation:

class lhc_zr_aitrip definition inheriting from cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  private section.

    methods get_global_authorizations for global authorization
      importing
        request requested_authorizations for Trip
        result  result.

    methods GetRecommendedValuesFunction for read
      keys for function Trip~GetRecommendedValuesFunction result result.

    methods build_recommendation_prompt
      importing title         type string
      returning value(result) type string.

    methods get_type_recommendation
      importing prompt        type string
      returning value(result) type string.

endclass.


class lhc_zr_aitrip implementation.

  method get_global_authorizations.
    " demo only: open for all users - add real authorization checks before productive use
    result-%create = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed.
  endmethod.

  method GetRecommendedValuesFunction.

    result = corresponding #( keys ).

    read entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
      entity Trip
        fields ( Title ) with corresponding #( keys )
      result data(trips)
      failed failed.

    loop at result assigning field-symbol(<result>).

      read table trips with table key id components %tky = <result>-%tky into data(trip).
      check sy-subrc = 0 and trip-Title is not initial.

      data(type_prompt)      = build_recommendation_prompt( conv #( trip-Title ) ).
      data(recommended_type) = get_type_recommendation( type_prompt ).

      check recommended_type is not initial.

      <result>-%param = value #(
        trip-type = value #( (
          score     = '1.0'
          value     = recommended_type
          suggested = 'X' ) ) ).

    endloop.

  endmethod.


  method build_recommendation_prompt.

    result = |Derive a trip category based on the given trip title: | &&
             |{ title }| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf &&
             |The following trip categories exist: C (Customer facing), I (Internal).| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf &&
             |Please only answer with 'C' or 'I' as a single character.|.

  endmethod.


  method get_type_recommendation.

    try.
        data(api)                = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'ZINTS_TRAVELAPP' ).
        data(message_container)  = api->create_message_container( ).
        message_container->add_user_message( prompt ).

        result = api->execute_for_messages( message_container )->get_completion( ).

      catch cx_aic_api_factory cx_aic_prompt_template cx_aic_completion_api.
        " recommendations are optional - on failure the field simply gets no suggested value
    endtry.

  endmethod.

endclass.

Step 3: Expose in the Projection

Make sure to expose the functionality in your UI projection by using “use recommendations;”. And that's it. The Fiori UI picks up the recommendation pattern automatically. No custom UI code, no frontend development, no begging a UI5 developer for help.

The Beauty of It

The beauty of RAP recommendations is the zero-effort UX integration. You implement the intelligence once in the behavior pool, and every Fiori Elements UI that consumes your RAP Business Object automatically benefits from the recommendations. It's the RAP philosophy at its finest: define the behavior, and the framework handles the presentation. And because the recommendation logic uses the ABAP AI SDK, you can switch from a deterministic rule-based approach to a generative AI approach (or vice versa) without changing the behavior definition or the UI. The abstraction is clean, the separation of concerns is real, and your future self will thank your present self for the architecture.

 

Use Case 2: Receipt Data Extraction

The Problem

After a business trip, the employee needs to submit expense reports with receipts attached. Hotel invoices, restaurant bills, taxi receipts. Today, the employee manually types in every field: vendor name, amount, currency, date, tax, category. It's tedious, error-prone, and, let's be honest, the reason most people procrastinate on their expense reports for weeks. Some of us have receipts from trips that happened so long ago that the ink has faded. Not speaking from personal experience, of course.

What if the employee could simply upload a receipt image and the system would extract the relevant data automatically?

Figure 2: AI-generated invoice

The Solution: Document Extraction with the ABAP AI SDK

This use case leverages the ABAP AI SDK's ability to send content, including file-based content, to an LLM and receive structured data back. The flow is:

  1. The user uploads a receipt (image) through the Fiori application.
  2. The ABAP application receives the file content.
  3. The ABAP AI SDK sends the file content along with a structured prompt to the LLM (via the Generative AI Hub).
  4. The LLM extracts key fields: vendor name, amount, currency, date, tax amount, expense category.
  5. The extracted data is returned to the ABAP application and pre-fills the expense line item.

The user uploads a crumpled taxi receipt, and five seconds later all the fields are filled in correctly. That's the kind of user experience that makes people actually submit their expense reports on time.

Figure 3: Extracted data from file

Step 1: Enhance the CDS Data Model for File Upload

Before we can extract anything, we need to give users a way to upload their receipts. In RAP, file uploads are modelled as Large Objects (LOBs) using the @Semantics.largeObject annotation in your CDS view. This tells the framework to treat the field as a binary stream and render it as a file upload control in the Fiori UI (SAP Help, Working with Large Objects). First, your database table needs three fields: the binary content itself, a MIME type field, and a file name field. Then, in your CDS entity, you annotate them accordingly:

@Semantics.largeObject: {
    acceptableMimeTypes: [ 'image/*', 'application/*' ],
    cacheControl.maxAge: #MEDIUM,
    contentDispositionPreference: #INLINE,
    fileName: 'UploadedReceiptFileName',
    mimeType: 'UploadedReceiptMimeType'
}
UploadedReceipt,

@Semantics.mimeType: true
UploadedReceiptMimeType,

UploadedReceiptFileName,

Let's break down what's happening here:

  • UploadedReceipt is the actual LOB field that stores the binary content of the uploaded file. The @Semantics.largeObject annotation binds it to its MIME type and file name fields, and defines which file types are accepted.
  • acceptableMimeTypes controls what the user can upload. In our case, image/* covers photos of receipts (JPEG, PNG, etc.) and application/* covers PDFs and other document formats. If you want to be more restrictive, you can specify individual MIME types like 'image/jpeg', 'application/pdf'.
  • UploadedReceiptMimeType stores the MIME type of the uploaded file and must carry the @Semantics.mimeType: true annotation. This is what the framework uses to know how to handle the file.
  • UploadedReceiptFileName stores the original file name. Technically optional, but very much recommended, because your users will appreciate seeing "taxi_receipt_berlin.pdf" instead of a cryptic binary blob identifier.
  • contentDispositionPreference: #INLINE tells the browser to display the file directly when possible (e.g. images and PDFs), rather than forcing a download.

Once these annotations are in place, the Fiori Elements automatically renders an upload control on the Object Page. No UI5 coding, no custom frontend logic. The user clicks upload, picks a file, and the binary content flows into your RAP Business Object. If you've ever implemented file upload the "classic" way in SAP, you'll appreciate how clean this is.

Step 2: Extract Data with the ABAP AI SDK

With the receipt uploaded and stored in the LOB field, the extraction can begin. The implementation combines the file content from the RAP entity with the ABAP AI SDK Completion API. You read the binary content from the LOB, and send it along with a structured extraction prompt through the SDK.

An execution flow could look like this:

  1. Read the uploaded receipt content from the entity (UploadedReceipt field)
  2. Convert to base64 encoding
  3. Build a structured extraction prompt:    
    'Extract the following fields from this receipt: vendor_name, amount, currency, date, tax_amount, category. Return the result as JSON'.
  4. Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API with the prompt and the file content
  5. Parse the JSON response
  6. Map extracted fields to the expense line item entity

The full implementation:

class lhc_expense definition inheriting from cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  private section.

    types: begin of ty_reference_lists,
             transaction_types type string,
             categories        type string,
           end of ty_reference_lists.

    methods extractData for determine on modify
      keys for Expense~extractData.

    methods get_reference_data_lists
      returning value(result) type ty_reference_lists.

    methods build_extraction_prompt
      importing reference_lists type ty_reference_lists
      returning value(result)   type string.

    methods call_ai_extraction
      importing receipt       type xstring
                prompt        type string
      returning value(result) type string
      raising   cx_aic_completion_api
                cx_aic_api_factory.

    methods parse_extraction_response
      importing json    type string
      changing  expense type any
      raising   cx_root.

endclass.


class lhc_expense implementation.

  method extractData.

    read entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
         entity Expense all fields with corresponding #( keys )
         result data(expenses).

    check expenses is not initial.

    data(reference_lists) = get_reference_data_lists( ).
    data(prompt)          = build_extraction_prompt( reference_lists ).

    data updates type table for update zr_aitrip\\Expense.

    loop at expenses assigning field-symbol(<expense>).

      if <expense>-UploadedReceipt is initial.
        append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                         %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                        text     = 'No receipt uploaded - nothing to extract' ) )
          to reported-expense.
        continue.
      endif.

      try.
          data(answer) = call_ai_extraction( receipt = <expense>-UploadedReceipt
                                              prompt  = prompt ).

          parse_extraction_response( exporting json    = answer
                                      changing  expense = <expense> ).

          append corresponding #( <expense> ) to updates.

        catch cx_aic_completion_api cx_aic_api_factory into data(ai_error).
          append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                           %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                          text     = |Receipt could not be processed by the AI service: { ai_error->get_text( ) }| ) )
            to reported-expense.

        catch cx_root into data(parse_error).
          append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                           %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                          text     = |Receipt data could not be interpreted: { parse_error->get_text( ) }| ) )
            to reported-expense.
      endtry.

    endloop.

    check updates is not initial.

    modify entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
       entity Expense
       update fields ( ExpenseDescription TransactionType Category Amount Currency )
       with updates.

  endmethod.


  method get_reference_data_lists.

    select transactiontype, description from zr_transactiontype into table @DATA(transaction_types).
    loop at transaction_types reference into data(transaction_type).
      result-transaction_types = result-transaction_types &&
        |{ transaction_type->transactiontype } ({ transaction_type->description }),|.
    endloop.

    select category, description from zr_category into table @DATA(categories).
    loop at categories reference into data(category).
      result-categories = result-categories && |{ category->category } ({ category->description }),|.
    endloop.

  endmethod.


  method build_extraction_prompt.

    result = |Analyze the attached receipt and extract the following information.| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |Do NOT wrap the response in markdown. Respond in valid JSON.| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |\{ | && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"TransactionType" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Category" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"ExpenseDescription" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Amount" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Currency" :""| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |\}| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |The following TransactionTypes exist in the system: { reference_lists-transaction_types }| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |The following Categories exist in the system: { reference_lists-categories }|.

  endmethod.


  method call_ai_extraction.

    data(api)               = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'ZINTS_TRAVELAPP' ).
    data(message_container) = api->create_message_container( ).

    message_container->add_user_media_message(
      )->add_media( aic_media_type=>image_webp
      )->set_media_data( cl_web_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( receipt )
      )->add_text( prompt ).

    result = api->execute_for_messages( message_container )->get_completion( ).

  endmethod.


  method parse_extraction_response.

    /ui2/cl_json=>deserialize( exporting json        = json
                                         pretty_name = /ui2/cl_json=>pretty_mode-none
                               changing  data        = expense ).

  endmethod.

endclass.

The extraction can be triggered as a RAP determination (automatically when the file is uploaded), as a RAP action (explicitly by the user pressing an "Extract" button), or even through an event-driven side effect that fires after the upload completes. All three options are valid RAP patterns, and the right choice depends on your UX preferences. Personally, I like the determination approach: the user uploads the file, and by the time they look at the form fields, they're already filled in. A small moment of delight in an otherwise tedious process.

Orchestration Adds Enterprise Readiness

This is where the orchestration capabilities mentioned earlier become critical. Receipts may contain sensitive personal data: credit card numbers, home addresses, personal phone numbers. By enabling Data Masking in the orchestration configuration, you ensure that such data is redacted before it reaches the LLM. No code changes required, it's a configuration in the intelligent scenario. Similarly, Document Grounding can be used to provide additional context to the LLM (for example, your company's expense categories and vendor master data), improving extraction accuracy significantly. The LLM doesn't just guess "Restaurant" as a category, it picks the exact category code from your company's chart of accounts.

The Beauty of It

Receipt extraction is a high-volume, low-complexity task that AI handles extremely well. Every minute saved on manual data entry is a minute your employees spend on work that actually matters. And because the extraction runs inside ABAP, not in an external service that your users need to learn, the integration is invisible. The user uploads a file, the fields fill themselves. That's it. That's the entire (very simple) user story.

 

Additional References

You want directly jump start into an own implementation? Go for it! In case any questions arise within this journey, feel free to check out the following additional references:

  • ABAP AI SDK, SAP Help
  • Set Up ABAP AI SDK powered by ISLM, SAP Help
  • Defining RAP Recommendations in the Behavior Definition, SAP Help
  • RAP Recommendations, SAP Community Blog
  • Implement a Simple Custom ABAP AI Scenario, SAP Developers Tutorial

 

Cheerio ABAP Folks!

entry.title: ABAP development tools MCP server: Major update available!
entry.content:
Introduction

The ABAP development tools MCP server shipping with the Eclipse plug-in and the VS Code extension is the official MCP server for ABAP development from SAP.  The new version adds a list of much needed tools which makes the server not rely on external tools such as read/edit from the VS Code chat anymore. This means it can now be properly used with all available CLI tools such as Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, OpenCode, .... This is a significant update which will change the way ABAP developers do agentic development with ABAP. In this blog post we want to provide an overview of the server, explain its architecture, the underlying design philosophies, the available features and how to best get started with using it.

General architecture

In general, the MCP server comes bundled with ADT for Eclipse or ADT for VS Code. It runs on the same Java codebase the normal tools run on. This means it "simply" exposes the existing ABAP tools via an MCP interface.

Advantages of this approach:

  1. A mature software stack - The Java codebase driving the server has been used in production for 15+ years.
  2. Compatibility handling - The MCP server supports all ABAP server releases until SAP NetWeaver 7.31 SP04. It runs on the same compatibility layer as ADT for Eclipse. It features support for detecting incompatibilities and will notify users when they need to upgrade to a newer version.
  3. Edge cases covered - It took us years to find and implement all the different edge cases needed for ADT for Eclipse. Features like SAP Solution Manager support, handling of systems in various states (upgrade, no editing allowed, ...) and especially the handling of all the possible error scenarios took quite some time to figure out and implement.
  4. Full connectivity stack - The server offers all connectivity options that ADT for Eclipse provides: RFC, HTTP.
  5. Client side caching - Over the last decade various caching solutions have been implemented on the ADT client side. These range from file caches for reading development objects to optimizing certain backend functionality by using stateful connections. This is the reason why the MCP tools are fast.

Features

System Connectivity

The MCP server re-uses the existing client connectivity stack:

VersionConnectivity configurationSupported connectivity type
ADT for EclipseSystem connections are maintained via ABAP projectsRFC (SSO, Password), Cloud (Http)
ADT for VS CodeSystem connections are maintained via ABAP destinationsRFC (SSO, Password), Cloud (Http)

Safety policy

The server follows a "safety by default" policy. This means everything is switched off by default. It is up to the user to switch on what is needed and manage the associated risks accordingly. It follows the same "human in the loop" principle which applies to AI in general.

Currently, the following configuration options are available:

  • Server switch - In Eclipse and VS Code the server is switched off by default and needs to be explicitly switched on.
  • System allow list - The user needs to specify which ABAP systems can be used.
  • Read only by default - The included ABAP object edit tool is switched off by default. VS Code users need to be aware that the VS Code chat edit tools need to be managed separately as they come from Microsoft.
  • No package allow-listed by default - All editing operations (Create, Edit, Delete [will be added at some point]) need to be allowed for specific packages by default.

The following diagram shows how users can gradually open up the available access.

Tools

Core philosophy:

  • As token efficient as possible - Every tool gets optimized for maximum efficiency while maintaining a solid out of the box experience.
  • As generic as possible - Re-use tools for multiple use cases.
  • Scales well - ABAP currently has 100+ object types. Even if it reaches 200+ object types the amount of MCP tools should stay the same e.g. one read tool for all objects, one tool for additional actions an object type might need (service binding needs a publish action), ...
  • Framework first - Most tools are built on frameworks and scale automatically e.g. the object creation tools do not need to be adjusted if a new object type gets introduced.
  • Solid out of the box experience - While AGENTS.md files can always be used to improve the performance of an agent, the tools shall work without any major custom instructions.
  • Integrates well with other MCP servers - The number one integration point between ABAP MCP servers are identifiers for objects. These can come in different types: name+type, URI, file path, ... Our server is built on the idea that the LLM can provide any valid identifier and the server does the mapping. This means community servers which might only offer one identifier work seamlessly with the ADT MCP server.

Supported tools

Tool IDDescriptionAdded with 1.2 release
abap_destination_listList available ABAP destinations 
abap_object_createCreate an ABAP object. Supports all object types which the new creation framework for VS Code supports 
abap_repository_list_creatable_typesList creatable object types 
abap_object_get_creatable_type_detailGet object metadata needed for creation 
abap_object_validate_creationValidate creation input 
abap_objects_generator_runGenerate objects 
abap_objects_generator_get_schemaGet generator schema 
abap_objects_generator_listList available generators 
abap_object_activateActivate ABAP objects 
abap_object_checkCheck ABAP objects for errorsYes
abap_object_list_actionsList available actions for an objectYes
abap_object_run_actionRun an action on an object. Besides actions which all objects support such as check, activate, lock, ... there are actions which are object type specific. One example is the service binding which has dedicated publish/unpublish actions. Currently, the service binding is the only object type which is already supported by the tool. In the future all object types will be supported.Yes
abap_object_get_document_symbolsSymbol map of a class/interface include. Basically the outline for a given object. It allows the LLM agent to first get a rough and token efficient overview before drilling down into the specificsYes

abap_object_edit_fileExact string replacement edit. Supports all object types which can be natively edited in ADT for EclipseYes

abap_object_list_file_urisList AFF files of an object e.g. class includesYes

abap_transport_get_requestGet/validate transport requests 
abap_transport_get_unified_diffUnified diff of a transport 
abap_unit_run_testsRun ABAP Unit tests 
abap_atc_run_get_resultGet ATC run result 
abap_atc_run_startStart an ATC run 
abap_atc_quickfixes_applyRun deterministic ATC quickfixes 
abap_atc_exemption_list_approversFind ATC exemption approversYes
abap_atc_exemption_requestCreate ATC exemption requestYes
abap_atc_ai_get_fix_resultCheck AI fix job status/result 
abap_atc_ai_start_fixApply AI fixes for ATC findings 
abap_business_service_get_infoFetch OData service info. Needed to build end-to-end Fiori applications in combination with the Fiori MCP server 
abap_business_service_listFetch services from a binding. Needed to build end-to-end Fiori applications in combination with the Fiori MCP server 
abap_feed_queryQuery an ABAP feed (FQL) e.g. shortdumps, gateway error logs, system messages, ...Yes
abap_feed_get_schemaGet ABAP feed schemaYes

Interoperability with other MCP servers or CLI tools

For all central ABAP development tasks such as CRUD support for objects or lifecycle management the official server should be the first choice. But the server will never satisfy all requirements and in this case additional servers or CLI tools are needed. This means the ADT MCP server needs to integrate nicely with the other solutions. The main integration point which we know is ABAP object IDs. A custom server might analyze an object and then want to use the ADT MCP server for reading additional object information. This needs to work seamlessly. Unfortunately, various forms of object IDs exist and we do not know which one is required. In order to solve this problem all our tools use a "oneOf" parameter which supports a range of object IDs.

Here the parameter description for the ABAP object identifier:

objectIdentifier (type oneOf): Identifies the ABAP object. Provide exactly one of:

- uri —> ADT URI (/sap/bc/adt/...), ADT Language Server URI, or SFS URI
- objectName + optional objectType —> e.g. CL_MY_CLASS with type CLAS
- affFileName —> AFF file name, e.g. cl_my_class.clas.abap

Recommended user journeys

How should an ABAP developer new to agentic development get started? The following paragraphs explain the recommended on-boarding path for such users.

Start with ADT for VS Code or ADT for Eclipse

From all the available options the user experience for ADT for VS Code is the most streamlined one.

  • The MCP server can be enabled with a single button click. No text based configuration needed.
  • All settings can be configured visually via the settings UI.
  • The chat UI makes it easy to configure the tools users need for their project.
  • The VS Code chat experience is polished and easy to use.

ADT for Eclipse is nearly as good. All settings can be done via a dedicated settings UI but the MCP server needs to be configured manually via a text based configuration.

For anybody who wants to experience agentic ABAP development for the first time the recommendation is to start with ADT for VS Code.

After the first steps connect the ADT for VS Code server to a CLI of your choice

 Here is a list of prominent CLIs:

  • Claude Code
  • OpenCode
  • Codex
  • GitHub Copilot CLI

All these CLIs work with the ADT MCP server. In order to enable the server a CLI specific configuration needs to be done. Just check the documentation for the respective CLI.

We recommend using the CLI next to your IDE. In this setup the MCP server process is attached to the IDE process. This setup allows developers to let agents run in the CLI and use the IDE to do code reviews, etc.

What's next?

Further development can be generally divided into two areas: 1) additional tools 2) refinement of existing tools. The following features are already planned. See roadmap for more information.

Refinement of existing tools

  • Support for coverage measurements when using the unit test run tool.
  • Improved destination tool. Providing additional metadata.
  • Improved object creation (adding missing object type support).
  • Improved read tool. Support of more extensibility artifacts.
  • ...

Additional tools

  • New source code search tool.
  • New where-used tool.
  • New tool for reading ABAP traces.
  • ...

Allow list improvements

Giving users the ability to provide individual settings for each destination.

Further information

  • Help page for the ADT MCP server
  • Roadmap information for ABAP AI related topics including the MCP server

entry.title: ABAP development tools for Visual Studio Code: Version 1.2 released
entry.content:
What happened since the last release?

Link to the extension.

Welcome back after the summer period! Hopefully you had a great time in the sun. We did not take a break and kept on working hard on the next version. It is available on the marketplace, now.

We heard your feedback. The additional object type support in version 1.1 made the extension a lot more useful for the ABAP developer community. With version 1.2 we continue this trend. It adds support for additional 23 object types. It features the first ABAP specific views and most importantly it updates the bundled MCP server with additional tools which will unlock the full power of all AI agents including Claude Code!

Some of you might wonder why this release took longer than the last ones. After the initial release we are now back to the regular three months rhythm that you know from ADT for Eclipse. It allows us to keep both products in sync and release new versions is parallel.

SAP TechEd Berlin is around the corner. We will have a demo station: „Build agents, workflows, and applications (AD)“. Stop by and have a chat. Let's talk VS Code, AI and how our tools can help you get things done!

 

What gets shipped with this release?

The following list only shows the major new additions. Of course, lots of smaller fixes, tweaks got added as well. See our what's new page for the full list.

Additional object type support

The following object types got added with full CRUD support:

Core ABAP
Transaction, Package, Software Components Relations, Transformation

CDS
Annotation Definition, Scalar Function Definition, Dynamic Cache, Static Cache, Entity Index

Data Dictionary
Data Element, Table technical settings

App Infrastructure 
Application Log Object, Archiving Object, Message Class, Background Processing Context, Application Job Catalog Entry, Application Job Template, Business Configuration Maintenance object

Fiori / UI
App Descriptor Item, Page Template, Space Template

Extensibility
BAdI Enhancement Spot, BAdI Enhancement Implementation, Predefined Field Enabling

Transport Organizer

First version of the transport organizer, so you can see and work with your transport requests without leaving VS Code.

ABAP feeds

First version of the feed reader for all available feeds such as short dumps, the gateway error log, system messages, ...

Timeline (Version history)

Lots of you requested this one. Version history view, letting you compare previous versions of an object.

entry.title: How abap2UI5 Complements RAP and Fiori Elements – Now Also as a Custom Control
entry.content:
With abap2UI5, a complete UI5 app is a single ABAP class – source code only, nothing else to create, generate or deploy. That gives a lot of freedom, and nothing is held back: the whole UI5 control library is available through XML views, built in ABAP. And under the hood, it is all standard technology: what runs in the browser is a normal UI5 freestyle app, and what runs on the server is plain ABAP on released APIs.

Which UI technology, and when?

Anyone who builds user interfaces on SAP knows the question. Classic screens or the newer UI technologies? And within the newer ones: RAP with Fiori Elements, Fiori Elements with developer extensibility, or a switch to UI5 freestyle? Each of these decisions is complex on its own, and every additional UI technology makes the landscape more complex, not less.

So where could abap2UI5 fit in?

Not a replacement – a complement

abap2UI5 is not here to replace any existing technology. The recommendation is simple: go with RAP and Fiori Elements as far as they take you. RAP is powerful: CDS views for the data model, a behavior definition for the business logic, a service binding, and with Fiori Elements on top a complete, consistent UI that SAP maintains – often with surprisingly little code. Where that fits, it is the right choice.

But there are places where a switch to abap2UI5 makes sense:

  • The data model does not map one to one onto a CDS model – the structure is only known at runtime, or the screen is a tool rather than a view on a business object.
  • The system runs on a release where RAP is not available yet.
  • A small screen is needed quickly – an admin tool, a correction screen, a dashboard for one team – and a full RAP stack would be more effort than the screen itself.
  • Developer extensibility has been reached, and the next step would otherwise be a UI5 freestyle app.

In those places abap2UI5 complements RAP and Fiori Elements. It does not compete with them – it is one more way to build a UI5 app, on the same technology. The best way to find out whether it fits: just try it.

Runs everywhere your ABAP runs

abap2UI5 runs on every release from NetWeaver 7.02 up to ABAP Cloud. The framework itself uses released APIs only, so it is ready for clean core – and whether an app is cloud-ready is decided by the app's own code, not by the framework.

Under the hood, abap2UI5 is nothing else than a normal UI5 freestyle app, ready to be deployed wherever UI5 apps run: on the ABAP system itself or on SAP BTP.

Open source, nothing to lose

abap2UI5 is open source under the MIT license. Trying it out costs nothing and does not bite. And if it does not fit, it can simply be deleted again, or just left unused.

How to start

Install abap2UI5 with abapGit in a few minutes – everything needed is in the installation guide.

Then there are several ways to develop:

  • Start in the browser. The abap2UI5 playground runs abap2UI5 entirely in the browser – no system needed. Write the first app there, get familiar with the basic behavior, then copy the class into the system and run it there. In a second step, add the business logic – and the first working app is done.
  • Design the screen first. For those who prefer visual screen design, the new layout designer is there to try: build the screen the way it should look, copy the app into the system and keep developing.
  • Learn from samples. The sample catalog has hundreds of ready-to-run apps, searchable by control and by UI5 release.

There is no vendor lock-in: an abap2UI5 app is pure ABAP code, in your own system, transportable like any other class – and easy to share with others.

Into production, next to your other apps

A finished app goes into production like any other: integrated into the SAP Fiori launchpad or SAP Build Work Zone as a tile. There, abap2UI5 apps live right next to your RAP and UI5 freestyle apps, and no end user sees a difference – because under the hood an abap2UI5 app is nothing else than a normal UI5 app.

New: abap2UI5 as a custom control

abap2UI5 does not only run as a full app. It now also comes wrapped in a UI5 custom control, which brings it right into the apps you already have: into a UI5 freestyle app, into a Fiori Elements app, and into the developer extensions of Fiori Elements – custom sections and custom pages.

 This fits the path a new app typically follows today:

  1. Start with RAP. CDS view entities, a behavior definition with validations, determinations and draft handling, a service binding, and a Fiori Elements app with list report and object page. As long as the annotations can express what is needed, stay here.
  2. When the backend cannot go further, use developer extensibility. Sooner or later a requirement comes along that the annotations have no word for – a credit check for one sales order that needs three function modules and a decision table, or a delivery simulation with a chart. Then the next step is a frontend project for the Fiori Elements app (for example with SAP Fiori tools) and its well-defined extension points: custom columns, custom actions, custom sections and custom pages. The list report, the object page, the draft handling and the navigation all stay where they are.
  3. Put abap2UI5 into the custom section. What used to go into such an extension was an XML fragment, a controller and JavaScript. Now the section can hold the abap2UI5 control instead – and its content is an ABAP class.

The control is z2ui5.embed.Container from the npm package @abap2ui5/embed-control.

One fragment, one class

A custom section is an entry in manifest.json (SAP Fiori tools generates it via the Page Map):

"SalesOrderObjectPage": {
  "type": "Component",
  "name": "sap.fe.templates.ObjectPage",
  "options": {
    "settings": {
      "contextPath": "/SalesOrder",
      "content": {
        "body": {
          "sections": {
            "creditCheck": {
              "template": "sales.order.ext.CreditCheck",
              "title": "Credit Check",
              "position": { "placement": "After", "anchor": "General" }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

and a fragment, which holds the control, bound to the sales order on the page:

<core:FragmentDefinition
    xmlns:core="sap.ui.core"
    xmlns:z2ui5="z2ui5.embed">
    <z2ui5:Container
        core:require="{ Section: 'sales/order/ext/CreditCheck' }"
        app="{ path: 'SalesOrder', formatter: 'Section.app' }"
        params="{ path: 'SalesOrder', targetType: 'any', formatter: 'Section.params' }"
        height="420px"/>
</core:FragmentDefinition>

Two small formatters decide which ABAP class runs and what it gets:

sap.ui.define([], () => {
  "use strict";

  return {
    app(order) {
      return order ? "ZCL_SALES_ORDER_CREDIT_CHECK" : "";
    },

    params(order) {
      return order ? { salesorder: order } : null;
    },
  };
});

That is all the JavaScript there is, and it does not grow: whatever the section does next is written in the class. Nothing starts before the page has an order, and navigating to the next order ends the running abap2UI5 session and starts a new one with the new number.

(targetType: 'any' is needed with OData V4: without it, the binding tries to convert the Edm.String key into the object type of params and fails.)

Importing parameters, e.g. the sales order

On the ABAP side the values arrive as startup parameters – think of them as the app's IMPORTING parameters. client->get( )-t_comp_params is a table of name and value, read once when the app starts:

METHOD z2ui5_if_app~main.

  IF client->check_on_init( ).
    LOOP AT client->get( )-t_comp_params INTO DATA(param).
      IF to_lower( param-n ) = `salesorder`.
        sales_order = param-v.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.
    " read the order, run the check, build the view
  ENDIF.

ENDMETHOD.

Every value arrives as a string, and any number of them can be handed over: the order number, the sold-to party, the sales organization. From there it is an ordinary abap2UI5 app. It reads the order with a SELECT, or through the RAP business object with EML – and then the validations, the draft and the authorizations of the business object still apply. The business logic stays in RAP; abap2UI5 only puts a different UI in front of it, for this one section.

Several apps side by side

Every control runs its own abap2UI5 session. Two sections with two containers are two apps with two independent states – a credit check and a delivery simulation for the same order, each a class of its own, each started with the same order number:

<z2ui5:Container app="ZCL_SALES_ORDER_CREDIT_CHECK" params="{ ... }" height="420px"/>
<z2ui5:Container app="ZCL_SALES_ORDER_DELIVERY_SIM" params="{ ... }" height="420px"/>

The same goes for a custom page: a view of its own in the app's routing, with as many containers as the page needs.

And in UI5 freestyle?

The control is an ordinary UI5 control, so it works in any freestyle app as well:

<mvc:View xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc" xmlns:z2ui5="z2ui5.embed">
  <z2ui5:Container app="Z2UI5_CL_UI5_APP_HI_WORLD" height="400px"/>
</mvc:View>

An existing freestyle app can take over individual screens or areas written in ABAP, without being rebuilt.

What it takes

In the UI5 or Fiori Elements app, three entries:

1. The dependency: npm install @abap2ui5/embed-control

2. ui5.yaml, so that ui5 build takes the control along:

builder:
  settings:
    includeDependency:
      - "@abap2ui5/embed-control"

3. manifest.json, the resource root of the control's namespace:

"sap.ui5": {
  "resourceRoots": { "z2ui5.embed": "./thirdparty/z2ui5/embed/" }
}

What it does not take: no launchpad target mapping, no controller extension, and no copy of the abap2UI5 frontend in the app. The control loads the frontend from the abap2UI5 service it talks to anyway (/sap/bc/z2ui5?z2ui5-bundle), so the frontend always has exactly the version of the backend.

On the system, abap2UI5 1.146.0 or later is needed. From that release on, an embedded abap2UI5 leaves the URL hash to the page it runs in, so the object page stays an object page after a roundtrip. The page and the abap2UI5 service have to share an origin, which is the case for every app deployed to the same system or routed through an approuter. The control supports UI5 1.71 and later, the same floor as abap2UI5 itself. Fiori Elements apps for OData V2 work the same way, with the control in an object page extension instead of a custom section.

Try it

  • The control: abap2UI5/embed-control, published on npm as @abap2ui5/embed-control
  • The examples: abap2UI5/samples-embed-control – a UI5 freestyle app, Fiori Elements apps for OData V4 and V2 with two abap2UI5 apps side by side on the object page, and a UI Integration Card for SAP Build Work Zone. They also run locally without an SAP system.
  • One abapGit pull: the branch rap installs a complete example on an S/4HANA system (2020 or later): a RAP service, a Fiori Elements app as BSP, and the abap2UI5 classes it starts from the object page.
  • The documentation: Fiori Elements Integration

Summary

RAP and Fiori Elements come first: RAP for the business logic, Fiori Elements for the standard UI, developer extensibility when the annotations cannot go further, and UI5 freestyle where the browser really has to be smart. These are great technologies, and they stay exactly where they are.

abap2UI5 is a complement to them – as a full app where a quick ABAP-only screen is the better fit, and now as a custom control right inside the apps you already run. No end user sees a difference, no vendor lock-in is added, and trying it costs nothing.

Which screen in your landscape would you rather write in plain ABAP? Share your thoughts in the comments. Feedback, issues and pull requests are always welcome on GitHub.

The whole project is developed by ABAP enthusiasts who share their knowledge and time – big kudos to all contributors to abap2UI5. Join the ABAP open source community and work with us.

Happy ABAPing! 🦖🦕🦣

entry.title: Agentic ABAP with MCP: what is really solving problems for you?
entry.content:
With the major update of the ABAP development tools MCP server, MCP for ABAP is no longer an experiment. It now works with Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and the other CLI tools, and many of us already use some kind of agent in daily ABAP work.

I have been building and using agents on top of the ADT REST API for a few months, in my own S/4HANA 2023 lab. Instead of another how-to, I would like to open a discussion: where does it really help, where does it fail, and what could we share as a community? My notes first.

1. The first explanation is often plausible and wrong

This is true for people and for agents. A classic: SQL 305 on a CDS view, "single-row query returns more than one row". The usual explanation is a to-one association that finds duplicates. In my lab that alone gave no error: a LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN from MARA to MAKT, for a material with 3 texts, returned 3 rows. The 305 only came with a scalar subquery that returned more than one row.

What I learned: wherever an explanation comes from, mine or the agent's, it gets reproduced in a sandbox before I believe it. The test is cheap, the wrong explanation is expensive.

2. Reading standard code is where it shines, if you know the limits

Following a call chain through the Gateway runtime classes, to see which DPC methods are really called, is a job of minutes for an agent and of an afternoon for me.

But tools can lie by silence. In my lab, the where-used list of /IWBEP/IF_MGW_CORE_SRV_RUNTIME showed one custom class and none of the SAP classes that I then saw using it in their source. And a text search across packages only covers what it really opened.

What I learned: an empty result is not proof that something doesn't exist. The agent must say what it did not search.

3. The system is the judge, but test the judge first

For code written by a model, I let the system decide: syntax check, ATC, ABAP Unit. Before trusting the judge, I give it two controls: the correct solution must pass, and a known mistake must fail (for example, the language condition in the WHERE instead of the ON of a text join). If the known mistake passes, "it compiles" is quietly becoming "it is right".

4. Context is the real cost

/IWBEP/CL_MGW_ABS_DATA alone has more than 8,000 lines of source. One whole read of a class like this fills a big part of the context, and everything after it gets slower and more expensive. In my own numbers, most of the cost was the model reading a big context again and again, not the answers it wrote. Reading one method, or searching first and reading after, is the habit that pays.

5. Human in the loop, by habit

Read only by default. Writes only in $TMP in my lab, and only after I say yes. Transports stay with a person. It is the same idea as the "safety by default" policy of the SAP server, and I think it is the right default for everybody.

What I would like to hear from you

  1. Which tasks really save you time today: investigation and reading, writing new objects, reviews, tests?
  2. Do you use the official ADT MCP server, a community server, or your own? What made you choose?
  3. How do you check what the agent tells you before you act on it?
  4. How do you deal with authorizations and transports when an agent can write?
  5. What would be worth sharing as a community: AGENTS.md patterns, prompts that work, or a set of "known hard" ABAP questions to test agents on?

If there is interest, I am happy to collect the answers in a follow-up.
